subtopic: WATERPROOF FOOTWEAR

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minisier of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WATERPROOF FOOTWEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table copies in English and in French of two tariff

Tabling of Reports
board reports. One, reference No. 121, relates to waterproof footwear and rubber-soled canvas footwear. The other, reference No. 126, relates to fluorspar. These reports were received from the tariff board last December and I authorized their release for public distribution at that time. They are now being tabled, together with transcripts of the evidence taken at the board's public hearings, pursuant to section 6 of the Tariff Board Act.
The contents of these reports are no doubt already familiar to those members who, for one reason or another, are directly interested in them. There may, however, be some members who have not yet had an opportunity to examine the reports. Accordingly I should like to say a word about each of them.
Reference No. 121 on waterproof footwear and rubber-soled canvas footwear was initiated by my predecessor and a first report thereon was received by him shortly before the 1957 election. In tabling that report in October, 1957, I pointed out that the board had not been asked for recommendations. For that reason I referred the matter back to the board with the request that in due course it make any recommendations that it might deem warranted regarding the retention or modification of the present duties.
Pursuant to this request the tariff board considered representations submitted by the Canadian rubber footwear industry relating to both the British preferential and the most favoured nation rates of duty on rubber boots and shoes and rubber-soled canvas footwear. With respect to rubber boots and shoes the industry requested that a new duty of 15 per cent ad valorem be imposed on imports from the United Kingdom and other British preferential sources, and that the present ad valorem duties under the most favoured nation and general tariffs be accompanied by specific minimum duties ranging from 30 cents to 95 cents per pair. With regard to canvas shoes with rubber soles the revised tariff treatment sought by the industry envisaged the introduction of specific minimum duties ranging from 55 cents to $1.25 per pair under the British preferential tariff and from 60 cents to $1.35 per pair under the most favoured nation and general tariffs.
In the report which I have just tabled the tariff board states that it was not persuaded on the basis of the evidence submitted that it would be warranted in recommending the adoption of the duties requested by the industry. It did not recommend any changes in either the wording or rates of duty in respect of the tariff items covering waterproof footwear and rubber-soled canvas footwear.

The report on fluorspar results from a reference which I sent to the board on September 24, 1957. Fluorspar is a product which has not attracted wide attention but which is of very direct concern in two Canadian localities. It is used extensively in the aluminum industry and in the iron and steel industry as a flux. Smaller amounts are used by Canadian producers of glassware, enamels and certain chemicals.
Canada's principal fluorspar mines are located at St. Lawrence, Newfoundland. The larger of these, Newfoundland Fluorspar Limited, supplies acid grade fluorspar to its parent company, the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited. The other, St. Lawrence Corporation of Newfoundland Limited, formerly shipped its entire production as concentrate to an affiliated company in the United States. Following the termination in 1957 of its affiliate's contract for United States stockpiling purposes, the St. Lawrence Corporation's mine has been closed.
Apart from Newfoundland Fluorspar Limited and the St. Lawrence Corporation of Newfoundland, Limited, the only other operating producer of fluorspar in Canada is, according to the report, Huntington Fluorspar Mines Limited, Madoc, Ontario. This firm mines, crushes and hand picks metallurgical grade fluorspar on a small scale.
In its report the tariff board says that at the hearings the St. Lawrence Corporation of Newfoundland and Huntington Fluorspar Mines proposed that the existing duty free entry of fluorspar be replaced by a duty of $10 per ton on all grades from all sources. This proposal was opposed by The Aluminum Company of Canada, which owns Newfoundland Fluorspar Limited, and by Canadian producers of glass, steel and chemicals.
The tariff board came to the conclusion that the closing of the St. Lawrence Corporation's mine was not primarily due to developments in the Canadian market, but rather to the fact that it could no longer sell in the United States market on which it has been entirely dependent.
With regard to the applicants' request for the imposition of a duty of $10 per ton, the board's majority opinion is to be found on page 36 of the report which I have just tabled. The relevant extract is as follows:
On the basis of the current fair market value, f.o.b. mine or mill in Mexico (the major source of supplies to Canada), a duty of $10 per ton-estimated by the president of St. Lawrence Corporation of Newfoundland as necessary to permit operations yielding a profit of about $5 per ton-would have an ad valorem incidence of something between 60 and 100 per cent. While a duty of $10 per ton would be in the nature of a bonanza to the relatively small operation at Madoc, it would very likely prove-in the opinion of the board-insufficient to

permit St. Lawrence Corporation of Newfoundland to compete with the Mexican product. On the other hand, it would be a burden upon the domestic users of fluorspar, especially to those industries competing in export markets.
The board accordingly has not made any recommendation for any change in the provisions of the tariff on fluorspar.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) asked me if I would be making any report to the house on the meetings at the beginning of last week of the joint United States-Canada committee on trade and economic affairs. I intimated at that time that if it were the wish of the house I would make a short report and table the communique which the committee authorized to be issued at the conclusion of its meetings.
May I, therefore, now table copies of that communique and say briefly that the meetings of the committee proceeded in Ottawa on January 5 and 6. On the part of the United States it was attended by Hon. Robert B. Anderson, secretary of the treasury; Hon. Fred A. Seaton, secretary of the department of the interior; Hon. Lewis L. Strauss, secretary of the department of commerce; Hon. C. Douglas Dillon, under secretary of state for economic affairs; Hon. Marvin L. McLain, assistant secretary, department of agriculture, as well as by a number of high officials from the departments concerned in the administration of the United States.
Canada was represented by my colleagues the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) and myself as well as our officials.
It had been expected that Mr. Dulles, the secretary of state of the United States and Mr. Benson, the secretary for agriculture, would be attending, but within a few hours of the meeting both of them were incapacitated, the one by illness and the other as a result of an accident.
The meeting was carried on in the most friendly and informal atmosphere. A very wide range of subjects came before us for discussion. These subjects included, of course, trade problems; even with the happy relations that exist between Canada and the United States there are still formidable trade problems.

Inquiries of the Ministry
On the part of the Canadian representatives the Canadian point of view with respect to the limitations imposed by the United States on imports of Canadian oil, lead and zinc, as well as certain aspects of United States agricultural surplus disposal policies, were plainly stated and vigorously pressed as was also the firm insistence of the Canadian government upon the fullest respect being extended to Canadian sovereignty in all its aspects.
A question was raised after the meeting concerning the range of subjects that came before the meeting, as to whether matters pertaining to defence purchasing came within the scope of the discussions. They did not, Mr. Speaker. There is another joint cabinet committee, the committee on defence, which embraces within its scope matters pertaining to defence purchasing.
I stress the very happy and extremely friendly and informal spirit which prevailed on the part of representatives of both countries. The meetings were useful. They provided an opportunity for a timely exchange of views, and it is the view of the Canadian government that the meetings served a very useful purpose.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table the preliminary report of the Fraser river board submitted to the governments of Canada and of British Columbia as of October 31, 1958.
As a result of its three years' study and based on data accumulated for several years by its predecessor, the Fraser river board has made a number of recommendations which deserve careful study by the responsible authorities. These range from expanding the program of collecting basic data regarding the Fraser river basin to multi-purpose development proposals for the basin.
One project, predicated on a partial development of the river and on dyking, offers hope of controlling the disastrous floods which the lower mainland of British Columbia has known. This project, which requires further examination, might achieve flood control on


practically a self-supporting basis and with no harm to the salmon industry. If the British Columbia government is disposed to have this matter further examined, the dominion government will consider such a suggestion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house I should like to make a brief statement regarding the situation in the human history branch of the national museum of Canada.
In June, 1956, a civil service competition was advertised to fill the position of director of the national museum which was to become vacant with the retirement in November of that year of Dr. Alcoclc, who was formerly its head. After the competition was launched but before the selection of a new director was made, the then government decided, in October 1956, to create two museums, a museum of natural history and a museum of human history. As a result of the civil service competition Dr. Loris S. Russell was appointed director of the natural history branch and Dr. Jacques Rousseau was appointed director of the human history branch.
There has not been and there is not now any difficulty whatever in the natural history branch. So far as the human history branch is concerned, it appeared in June 1958 that there was serious unrest among the senior scientific personnel. An inquiry was immediately undertaken at the direction of the deputy minister. In the course of the inquiry, it developed that the director of the human history branch was in immediate need of two months' leave of absence for medical reasons. This, along with absences of the scientific staff in the field during the summer and fall, as well as absences by the deputy minister and myself on departmental business, delayed completion of the inquiry.
The inquiry has involved the interviewing of a great many people, the checking of many statements, and the examination of a great deal of material that has been submitted. Before it was completed the matter became the subject of reports in the press. The fullest inquiry has now been completed, and a report was submitted to me by my deputy minister on January 15.
May I say at this point, Mr. Speaker, that the report is confidential and it deals, on the basis of confidence between an official and his minister, with many complaints about and

reflections on the personalities and character of many people. As such it is a privileged document and it will not now nor, so far as I am concerned, at any time in the future be made public. A copy has, however, been sent to the chairman of the civil service commission for his information and retention.
From the most thorough inquiries it is clear that there are no policy questions of any kind at issue. It is purely and simply a case of violent clashes of personalities. There had, it is apparent, been certain strains among some of the scientists in the branch in the past, but these had never led to difficulties nor assumed serious proportions until now.
The inquiry has revealed that several scientists in the museum have been at fault in the matter in varying degrees. At my direction the deputy minister is interviewing these persons to make clear the deficiencies of conduct that have contributed to the most regrettable flare-up. It will be made abundantly clear to all of these that they will be expected henceforth so to conduct themselves in their relations with one another as to restore to the branch and to maintain in the future the atmosphere that is essential if the scientific work of the museum is to be carried on.
The director of the branch, Dr. Rousseau, is an ethno-botanist of wide reputation. I want it to be perfectly clear that nothing in the matter or in the inquiry or report has at any time or in any way reflected on his reputation or standing as a scientist. The direction of a branch of the museum is not, however, primarily a scientific task. It is primarily administrative. The inquiry has made it clear that Dr. Rousseau's talents are scientific rather than administrative. He is therefore being offered a purely scientific post in the public service which I hope he will see fit to accept. A period of time has been given Dr. Rousseau to consider the matter, and I would not wish to go further at this point.
The civil service commission has been consulted and kept fully informed before decisions were taken. They fully concur in the conclusions that have been reached.
I should like to add, Mr. Speaker, that as no question of policy is involved and as this is purely a matter of personal and internal frictions within the human history branch, I think it would be in the interest of the museum, of the public service, and of the scientists concerned if the healing processes of time could go forward as quietly and with as little further publicity as it is possible for them to do.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY INQUIRY AS TO READINESS FOR 1959 NAVIGATION SEASON

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY INQUIRY AS TO READINESS FOR 1959 NAVIGATION SEASON
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Will the minister advise the house concerning the readiness of the St. Lawrence seaway system to handle traffic at the commencement of the 1959 navigation season?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY INQUIRY AS TO READINESS FOR 1959 NAVIGATION SEASON
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I wish to thank the hon. member for his courtesy in advising me of his intention to ask this question. I shall make the following answer in view of the great interest shown in this matter by the hon. members for Vaudreuil-Soulanges, Glen-garry-Prescott and Grenville-Dundas.
At the end of 1958, just four and a half years after the St. Lawrence seaway authority was established, construction of works under


its jurisdiction has progressed to a stage which assures that all channels, locks and ancillary structures will be available to shipping at the opening of navigation next spring, although subject in part to a restricted depth of 24J feet until June 1, when the specified minimum depth of 27 feet will be available throughout.
An over-all insufficiency of equipment suitable for dredging of the various classes and conditions of materials encountered, aggravated by the early advent of winter which so seriously interfered with the clearing of ocean vessels from the Lachine canal and Montreal harbour, has retarded the completion of production and clean-up dredging and the proving of all navigation channels to the specified 27 feet depth and, in a few places, to full width.
All five lock structures undertaken by the seaway authority have been completed and all lock equipment and machinery has been installed and tested. All the work undertaken by the St. Lawrence seaway authority with respect to Jacques Cartier bridge, Victoria bridge, Honore Mercier bridge, Caughnawaga C.P.R. bridge and the Cornwall island high level bridge has been virtually completed. The St. Louis span for the Canadian National and the Valleyfield span for the New York Central over the Beauharnois canal are scheduled for completion by March 15, 1959. The Cornwall north channel bridge is scheduled for completion late in 1960, with tenders for the substructure to be advertised by the end of February, 1959. The seaway authority is issuing a more detailed statement as to completion of various phases of the work.
Before vessels may safely transit the new seaway facilities aids to navigation have to be placed, and this is a responsibility of the Department of Transport. Every effort will be made to have this work completed as closely as possible to the time when navigation normally would commence. This is dependent of course on weather, ice conditions, and a number of related factors. The present objective for the completion of this work is about April 20. However, in accordance with established canal operation practice a more precise statement as to the opening date can be expected toward the end of March.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable trepidation that I venture to make my contribution to this debate following the heavy artillery of
84	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. McGee yesterday, the sounds of which still seem to echo through this chamber. I should like to express my personal pleasure at finding you still in the chair. I should like further to add my congratulations to those which have already been expressed to your deputy, the chairman of committees, and to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address, and to say that I am happy to see that my admiration for the hon. member for Provencher is now being widely shared in this house. As for the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet, there is very little I can add to the universal praise and acclamation he has received from all corners of this house and in every newspaper I have been able to read since his speech was made.
I agree with everything that has been said, Mr. Speaker, concerning the speeches of the mover and seconder. There is one other comment I have to make about the tone of those speeches and their constructive aspect. The benefits which will accrue as a result of the suggestions made will continue for a long time to come. I might add, however, that the tone of the debate changed sharply when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) rose to his feet yesterday.
Referring to battles best forgotten, and taking a narrow partisan view of the various problems facing this country, I am happy to say he reaped the whirlwind later in the day. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had no choice but to reply in kind to that type of speech and to destroy the flimsy structure of those partisan arguments. I mentioned heavy artillery. As we know from experience in the last war, the heaviest artillery barrage still leaves a job to be done by the infantry.
I should like to take issue with the Leader of the Opposition concerning statements made to the people of Canada by members of the Conservative party concerning tight money. I suggest that he examine the record previous to the 1957 election in the riding of York-Scarborough and in every other riding I visited during the election. He would find it was the discriminatory effects of the tight money policy as applied by the Liberal government which were under fire, the fact that the small businessman bore the brunt of that policy. It was not a blanket condemnation of tight money or monetary policies.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to the famous white paper which appeared and disappeared presumably in the same drawer as the famous Canada medal, and other Liberal schemes. A notable feature of that white paper, as I recall it, was the shelf of public works. As I have stated in this house -and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) did not disagree with me-that shelf


did not exist, and was not available when needed by the present government.
I found it passing strange to listen to the Leader of the Opposition yesterday and his comments in general about government action concerning recession and inflation. I recall that in a television broadcast he referred in detail to this subject. We do not have the benefit of a staff to sit in front of television sets and make notes, but I do recall specific questions being put to the Leader of the Opposition on that program early in December asking him if there was anything he had to propose in the anti-recession field which the government had not already done; and his answer, as I recall it, was no. He was then asked whether there was anything which the government was doing with which he disagreed, and the answer to that question was also in the negative. I found it passing strange to hear the comments in the economic field yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition in such dramatic contrast to his statements to the nation in a television interview.
He has accused the government of adopting policies in fighting this recession which he characterized as fumbling and bumbling. I would like to take the Leader of the Opposition to my riding and to many other ridings in this country and show him low cost homes, low rental homes, homes that have been built and are now being constructed for the senior citizens of this country, homes being built for young families, homes they can afford to buy and maintain, as a result of these fumbling and bumbling policies. I ask the hon. gentleman if he disagrees. Would he prefer not to have seen these policies implemented which have had what I consider a tremendously beneficial result?
We will hear from hon. gentlemen opposite the words "fumbling" and "bumbling" in relation to almost every department of government in respect of their active anti-recession activities, and I may be permitted to anticipate just a few of the departments that will be subjected to this type of criticism. As long ago as December 1, 1958, the Minister of Public Works announced that jobs for 250,000 Canadians would be provided this winter by the government's housing program. I submit you cannot separate the on-site activities of building from the effect of such construction on the rest of the economy. One must consider the myriad items that have to be manufactured to supply these homes and furnish them when built and occupied. A conservative estimate of the potential indirect employment that could flow from that program is at least as much as the on-site employment, another quarter of a million jobs, and one-quarter of a million and one-quarter of a million make half a million jobs.

We move further into the government's own construction program, which will provide on-site employment this winter for 150,000 men. Certainly the ratio in that type of construction has far wider effects on the rest of the economy, but let us consider just a conservative estimate of 150,000 indirect jobs, or a total of 300,000 jobs, indirect and onsite.
We could go from department to department considering the beneficial results of the acceleration of anti-recession activities undertaken by this government and come to impressive totals which I am not prepared to present at this time. These are but a few of the examples of effective anti-recession activities which by no stretch of the imagination can be described as fumbling and bumbling.
Scarcely any item escaped bombardment yesterday in the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition, but from that torrent of words there emerged what is surely one of the most fascinating definitions of Liberalism ever to have been formulated. Hon. gentlemen may perhaps recall these words of the Leader of the Opposition uttered yesterday and reported at page 33 of Hansard of yesterday's date:
Certainly no Liberal can be anything but a champion of the rights and liberties of the free man against dictates and pressures, from whatever source they may come.
I wonder where were these brave fighters for Liberalism when the dictates and pressures of Mr. C. D. Howe steamrolled certain measures through this house? Where were these brave fighters for Liberalism at the time of a certain division that I recall very well in the 1957 session, when we saw brave Liberals flitting back and forth behind the curtains fearful because they might have won a vote?
I expected from the Leader of the Opposition something of a more positive and constructive nature with respect to the serious economic situation which confronts this country. I have a theory formulated from my studies of parliamentary history in Canada. I call it the "middle year" theory. Parliament is at its best and does its most effective work in the years between elections. In the session immediately following an election there is perhaps too much acrimonious debate with hon. members reminding each other of what might have been said in the heat of debate on the hustings. In the session before an election perhaps too many of us speak too much to the electorate and too little to each other in creative consultation concerning the issues at hand. Certainly if at any time we can have the calm and considered judgment of the representatives of the ridings in this country it should be in these middle years.
The Address-Mr. McGee
I looked forward earlier this session to having such a spirit prevail. This was destroyed completely yesterday by the tone and manner of the Leader of the Opposition when he spoke as I submit he did to the detriment of the deliberations of this house. I say further that we in this chamber would receive the thanks of a grateful nation if we set our minds to the serious tasks confronting us, particularly in the economic field, in seeking constructive solutions to these problems which is surely the highest function of parliament.
I have a few suggestions to offer, and perhaps I may be permitted to voice them. My first reference, of course, must be a plea for a less partisan approach to these difficult problems. Second, I would urge the instigation of a study which may already be under way to equalize the effects of monetary policy to prevent a recurrence of the discriminatory type of effects of the tight money policy of the previous administration, and to protect the small businessman from the squeeze. I also think we would do well to give serious consideration to a more flexible fiscal policy. It has been demonstrated fairly clearly that there are limitations to economic predictions and their accuracy. Great care however should be taken to retain the prerogatives of parliament in this regard.
I would also plead for the retention of the more important and favourable aspects of the housing program which has proven to be so effective as a monetary and fiscal policy. If this should be reduced in years to come when we are involved in another type of battle we will have lost the beneficial aspects of such a program which should be retained. I refer again to low cost housing, low rental housing, housing for senior citizens and urban redevelopment schemes.
As I have said before in this house, we have a form of recession each winter in Canada. These housing programs, particularly in the fields I mentioned, could be related to solving the problem of our annual winter recession. I have seen in my own riding, as I am sure many hon. members have seen in theirs, new construction techniques being adopted. Encased in envelopes of plastic polyethylene film, building can go forward in spite of severe temperatures outside. The adoption of such techniques and the application of new materials in the housing field make it possible for the continuation of an effective construction program despite the Canadian winter.
It was suggestions of this type that I expected to hear-and I hope we will hear many more from hon. members of all parties

The Address-Mr. Badanai in this house-during the course of this session. I should like to have heard similar suggestions from the Leader of the Opposition yesterday.
I was particularly disappointed but perhaps not surprised when the hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. Argue) took the floor yesterday and commenced with the typical pious and sanctimonious denunciation of the government and official opposition. But as I listened to him I wondered where was the brave leader of that group who, speaking on a platform in his home province not long ago, castigated and denounced the Prime Minister while gesturing wildly and wheeling his arms around the world. Surely the hon. member for Assiniboia does not lack the moral fortitude to face the Prime Minister with the type of accusation he had made in his home province; but though I expected to hear something of this kind yesterday there was no mention of it by the hon. member.
I expected to hear something about the reaction of westerners to the situation in his own party which was referred to yesterday in the press. It said that active members are splintering away from the Manitoba C.C.F. party because of the methods being used to create the new political party. I expected to hear something of the platform and program of this new and vital party which it is hoped will receive farm support. Who knows; perhaps this new platform was placed in the same dark spot as the Regina manifesto and other such statements.
There was in the hon. member's speech, I submit, Mr. Speaker, an indication that a little meeting was held. If I had the ability to write a dramatic account of that meeting, Mr. Speaker, I would say that what went on was this. One hon. member said, "I will shout about unemployment; you shout about inflation; we will both shout good and loud." No matter what the government does it is damned if it does and damned if it does not. I do not think the people of Canada will be misled by that shallow subterfuge. I think they know that when the battle of the recession has been won, as it will be won in the very near future, this government will come to grips with the battle of inflation; and further, that the vigorous and aggressive qualities that characterize this government will win that battle of inflation. Of that let there be no doubt.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin with a word of commendation for the way in which you perform your duties. You were the recipient of many compliments and congratulations when you were appointed Speaker of the house.

I recall that at our last session every member had a word of satisfaction on your appointment, and as a new member I joined my colleagues in expressing my sincere appreciation. However, it was not until I became better acquainted with the rules of the house that I began to realize the importance of an impartial Speaker.
I recall one instance when I offered an amendment on the second reading of a bill making changes in the Income Tax Act. My amendment called for consideration being given to repeal or reduce the excise tax on motor cars. The Minister of Finance submitted that the amendment was out of order, but after listening to the arguments you allowed the debate to proceed and it was put to a vote, notwithstanding the embarrassment to the government when it was reminded of past Conservative statements and promises compared with performance. On that occasion you earned the reputation of a worthy holder of the high office which you occupy and I trust that you will remain in the chair for a long time, irrespective of the political party which may be in power, for I hardly anticipate that this government will remain in power beyond the foreseeable future.
I also wish to say that I found the Deputy Speaker and the deputy chairman of the committee of the whole worthy of occupying their respective offices.
The mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne certainly deserve congratulations for their excellent presentations, and I certainly hope their expectations regarding the contents of the address will be justified. For my part, I feel that the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition (Mr. Pearson) has made a much clearer analysis of the speech, and I am forced to the conclusion that the government is still unsettled in its policies to meet the many important issues the solution of which is vital to the restoration of an economic climate of confidence, which this nation enjoyed in the postwar period under a Liberal administration.
In its general terms the speech contains some features which are welcomed by most Canadians, such as the reference to the discussions taking place with the government of the United States to enable Canadian industry to share in the production of equipment for joint defence purposes, which I trust will help especially the unemployment situation which is very serious in my constituency. When I say this I do not mean to be a spreader of fear. The situation is threatening to become worse unless the government will do something to ensure the continued operation

of the Canada Car plant, which is manufacturing buses and tractor traitors at the present time. The president of the company made the statement in Fort William recently that the decision had been made to transfer all their commercial operations to the Dominion plant in Montreal, and to dispose of their Fort William plant. This announcement was a sad blow to the economy of the entire lakehead. It aroused the entire community, with the result that on January 8 a large delegation from the lakehead met with the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Green) and other ministers to discuss the seriousness of the situation.
I must say that we were cordially received and were given a good hearing, for which I thank the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green), the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), and their respective deputies. Promises of consideration were given, and the delegation left the capital with a feeling that something had been accomplished. I sincerely hope that what the Prime Minister said last night, namely "the stronger the lobby the weaker the case" will not apply in this case. I express the hope that the government will make sure that this plant, which during the last war designed and produced Grumman fighter planes, the Gregory dive bombers and the Hawker Hurricanes and, since the war, the Harvard trainers, street railway cars, electric coaches, gas and diesel buses, Arctic huts for the United States army, tractor trailers, including heated and refrigerated models, will receive immediate consideration in the light of national interest.
The speech makes reference to an increase in Canada's contribution to the Colombo plan. We are all in favour of it, but why should this increase not be made in kind, such as with farm implements? This is a suggestion made by Senator N. M. Paterson to me, which if implemented could induce manufacturers such as Massey-Harris to manufacture these implements in the Canada Car plant in Fort William. Such an enterprise would not be subject to the uncertainties of defence orders to keep the plant in operation. It would also supply all our western farmers with machinery on a permanent basis which, after all, would be more desirable than the relatively short term operation of defence production. I am putting forth this idea as an alternative which I feel has merit.
The Address-Mr. Badanai
It pleased me to notice that at last the government has recognized the justice of granting supplementary pensions for retired civil servants and R.C.M.P. members on a permanent basis. Last year I had a resolution on the order paper in support of this measure.
In connection with the clause in the speech from the throne dealing with the establishment of a joint committee of both houses to review the Indian Act, I offer the suggestion that the government should give serious consideration to showing a more sympathetic approach toward the welfare of our Indian population. We have been all too prone to overlook some of their inherent rights in the past and to treat them indifferently. The Indians should not be treated as second-class citizens. Their record in our armed services during the first and second world wars was second to none.
In so far as housing is concerned, there does not seem to be any decline in the demand. Indeed, this is one item for which the demand is on the increase year by year. All one has to do is add up all the marriages taking place in these communities, and then it is easy to calculate the future requirements for housing. The natural increase in population, added to the number of new immigrants, creates a constant demand for low cost housing which the industry is not able to satisfy without government assistance to prospective homebuilders by way of loans at a low rate of interest on houses costing $12,000 or less. I suggested last year that a 2 per cent subsidy on prevalent rates of interest be considered for this type of home.
The reference to the housing problem in the throne speech falls rather short of expectations, since the need for dwellings to rent is so great that mere encouragement is not enough. We are faced with an unemployment situation which is critical, and anything that is said to the contrary will not make the thousands of unemployed in my constituency any happier. While an increase in tempo in the house-building industry will not be a cure-all for the ills caused by unemployment, it will at least create jobs in many fields. I am not a pessimist and there has never been depression in my vision, but at the same time I do not share all the optimistic predictions which have been made by members of the government concerning the easing of unemployment. Nothing would please the members on this side of the house more than to see the end of unemployment, but until we see a better picture it appears to me to be our duty to point up the need for transposing those rosy predictions into actuality.

The Address-Mr. Badanai
Having served as mayor of the city of Fort William for eight years, I was delighted to hear that parliament will be asked to assist the municipalities of Canada in financing construction projects. I hope this aid will not be limited to the recently announced winter work program in conjunction with provincial governments. In this connection it may interest you to know that this project has only benefited 120 unemployed in the city of Fort William. I express the hope that the assistance will go beyond the presently prescribed limitations.
One of the best forms of assistance to municipalities of which I know would be the establishment of a fund to be used for making loans directly to municipalities at a low rate of interest to finance the construction of essential public works such as sidewalks, sewers, pavements, bridges and schools. Another form of assistance would be the extension of tax relief on municipal purchases. During the last session the government removed the tax on certain purchases such as fire apparatus and road-building equipment. Municipalities should be exempt from all taxes on purchases of equipment and motor vehicles used by the works, engineering and police departments. The federal government could assist municipal councils by recognizing the combined provincial and municipal expenditures for the construction of technical and vocational secondary schools, and by making additional funds available to share in these costs.
Of all the legislation proposed by the Prime Minister none has received so much attention through all the known media of our times as has the bill of rights, which was introduced in parliament during the last days of the last session. There is indeed no shortage of arguments, pro and con, but there seems to be an area of general agreement in the fact that our laws and our courts have always protected our individual liberties guaranteed under our constitution. I am not a lawyer and I do not profess to be in a position to enlighten the house on what may be hidden behind the high-sounding words which appear in abundance in this document. Of course I am all for the things for which it is supposed to stand. After reading about the postmaster of a small sub-post office in York township who was dismissed because of a letter written to a newspaper criticizing the Prime Minister, I would say that the bill of rights falls far short of guaranteeing a man's freedom of expression if vocal expression of a political belief is involved.
So far as I am concerned the Postmaster General's statement that the Liberal administration fired 325 post office personnel

since 1935 is not the slightest excuse for meting out such inhuman treatment to employees. This is an action which contravenes any and all rights of free speech and assembly, and is in direct contradiction of the rights in the bill outlined so ceremoniously by the Prime Minister himself in the last days of the last session. If there is a right which should be guaranteed to every man and woman by this government, it is the right to free expression of opinion, even on the political platform, whether he or she is employed by private enterprise or by government. You may laugh if you wish; it is quite all right.
This is one of the most fundamental rights which should be respected regardless of whether or not there have been precedents approved by any government in the past, whether Liberal or Conservative. This government would render a great service to the whole country if it would come out with a declaration that in future there will be no dismissals of any members of the civil service or discrimination shown to anyone because of political activities, so long as those activities do not conflict in any way with the performance of their duties. Without this freedom of action this proposed bill of rights becomes nothing more than a document full of words without meaning.
If we must have a bill of rights-and I am certainly not opposed to it-let us have a bill which will spell out its meaning and which will include the declaration that no person shall be discriminated against because of political affiliations or activities, and which will apply to all persons including those in the employ of the government. Such an addition would give the bill substance, and I would be the first to stand up and cheer for it.
Nineteen years ago Stephen Leacock, in his history of Canada, had this to say about northwestern Ontario:
Perhaps the brightest page in these annals is the record of discovery and exploration of the incalculable mineral wealth of the central wilderness of Canada between the Hudson bay and the lakes. This means far more than the wealth itself, great though it must be. It removes from our commonwealth its fatal geographical defect of an uninhabited and seemingly worthless central area which broke east and west apart forever. The touch of King Midas is turning desolation into fairyland.
Since the great Canadian writer made this statement, northwestern Ontario has made considerable progress in the development of mines and forest products which has created a great industry, hydroelectric power will soon reach one million horsepower, and there is even a growing farm area. Also new communities have sprung up on the map of this great northern area.

I admit that the Prime Minister's vision of expanding and developing the country's northern regions to unlock its wealth of natural resources has captured the imagination of many Canadians. I submit that our federal government need not seek the very far north of Canada in order to apply this policy of development. The lakehead area in the very centre of Canada from lake Superior to Hudson bay and James bay is the very challenge to the imagination which our Prime Minister is seeking. No railway serves our region north of latitude 50 degrees. No highway goes beyond the Albany river and Red lake. In this vast territory the population averages one person per square mile. That is the situation right in the centre of Canada. What an opportunity there is for the government to open up central Canada with a railway and highway to connect the fresh water coast of lake Superior and the salt water bays of Hudson and James, tapping natural resources for nearly one thousand miles between them; to encourage and assist a new wave of settlement with a selective hardy stock of immigrants, creating new jobs, bringing more people and more wealth and developing strength and security for the whole of Canada.
This great area with the lakehead as its pivot, soon to become an ocean port, is awaiting the construction by the federal government of a modern harbour which has been promised. Notwithstanding divergencies of opinion with regard to the location of the proposed installations, when finally competent engineers decide on the site on its merits, solely from the standpoint of service to the whole area, then objections will vanish and the people at the lakehead will feel relieved from further uncertainties.
One cannot speak of the harbour without expressing disappointment at the delay in the appointment of the harbour commission, for which delay the government tried to blame the two city councils of Fort William and Port Arthur. These two cities appointed their members last July, only to be told later that the appointments were not valid because the bill to establish the lakehead harbour commission had not obtained royal assent.
I express the sincere hope that what the Prime Minister has in mind in his reference to the discrimination in respect of freight rates is to alleviate the discriminatory effects of the freight rate boost on the lakehead. We can all agree that the 17 per cent freight rate increase recently granted to the railways by the government was requested for the express purpose of meeting the wage increases demanded by the unions concerned. This being the case, I cannot help but consider
The Address-Mr. Badanai it most unfair to areas such as the lakehead which is approximately 850 rail miles from Toronto.
The distances between our centres of population and between industries are great. Freight rates are a big factor in the industrial development of northwestern Ontario. In the matter of grain movement and the transfer of goods between west and east, we are much more closely connected with Winnipeg and western Canada than with the east. Indeed, our economy is linked more closely with that of the province of Manitoba than with that of the eastern part of the province of Ontario.
I am sure my colleagues from northwestern Ontario will be as pleased as I was to learn that the government intends to spend more money than it has spent previously upon the trans-Canada highway. Because of the deplorable conditions of the trans-Canada highway from Fort William west to the Manitoba border many of our citizens are compelled to travel to Winnipeg via the United States. Quite recently the engineering experts employed by the Department of Transport predicted that from 50 to 100 transport trucks will be leaving the lakehead for the west every day once the lakehead seaway terminal is completed. I would most sincerely urge that sufficient funds be provided by the government to have this portion of the trans-Canada highway completed and ready to receive the increased traffic expected.
I wish to speak now on one aspect of national defence which concerns the city of Fort William. I refer to the Fort William armoury, which ceased operation on the 15th of this month. The building was formerly a hockey arena. It was purchased by the Department of National Defence in 1942 for $14,000. It was originally erected in 1919 at a cost of $40,000, and was of frame construction with timber beams and trusses. The property was owned by local residents who incorporated and were shareholders in the Fort William Arena Company.
Fort William previously had an armoury in a commercial block in the downtown area of the city. The facilities provided there were rather confined. In 1942 the need for a real armoury to train the reserve force became so acute that the Department of National Defence purchased the arena as a temporary expedient. In 1951 the council of the corporation of the city of Fort William offered a site to the Department of National Defence for a new armoury in a very central and suitable location. This site was offered on an exchange basis for the present armoury site. On July 26, 1954, a communication was

The Address-Mr. Badanai received from headquarters, prairie command, from which I quote:
Army headquarters have now advised us that your proposed site is satisfactory to the Department of National Defence. Army headquarters propose to take no further action until the treasury board approve the construction of the armoury in Fort William after which the exchange of lands as outlined by you will be arranged. Army headquarters have requested that the proposed agreement cover the use of the old armoury by the Department of National Defence until the new armoury is completed.
That letter was signed by N. E. Rodger, major general, in command of the prairie command. Sir, the armoury is now closed and the units will be transferred to the Port Arthur armoury. No consideration has been given to the status of the present armoury other than declaring it surplus and transferring it to war assets for disposal.
The city of Fort William objected strenuously to this procedure, for the land on which the armoury now stands is required by the city of Fort William to serve the Fort William Gardens, a large community centre adjacent to the armoury. Consideration has been given to providing accommodation for the cadet units which have been using the armoury ever since it opened, but no consideration is being given at the present time. These units comprise approximately 350 secondary school students who have been training regularly and are now deprived of the accommodation. This will mean that the present strength will eventually disintegrate, as there is no other suitable building to serve the purpose.
Last November I, as mayor of the city, sent a brief to the Minister of National Defence, but the only response received so far has been an acknowledgement. I submit on behalf of the city of Fort William that it has a right to expect some consideration of its proposal, and I trust that the minister will take another look at the situation because I am confident that he will be convinced that a city of 43,000 people guarding the granary of the nation should not be without the facilities to train our young men to take their proper places in the event of an emergency.
I am an ardent advocate of any measure that will bring about the establishment of a loan fund to assist those on undeveloped farms, especially in northwestern Ontario and other similar areas requiring hardy and dedicated people to make a success of such projects. We have that type of people in the district of Thunder Bay, but they find it difficult to obtain loans from established banks.
It seems to me that there should be a liberalization of the act governing the Canadian farm loan board. As an example, I have


received several letters from Mr. Gerhard Klinge of Walmsley, a township in my constituency. This chap came to Canada from Germany in 1951. He is married and has four boys ranging from 4 to 18 years in age. In 1954 he bought a homestead in the township of Pearson, and in 1957 he bought a neighbour's farm of 160 acres. With this farm he bought 10 cows as well as some farm equipment. In his spare time he worked in bush camps, and the monthly income of this hard working man from all sources was approximately $500, most of which was being used to make payments on mortgages and equipment. He required a loan of $8,000 and applied to the Canadian farm loan board. He even had the recommendation of the local agricultural representative. The loan was refused on the ground that his income was not sufficient to meet his obligations.
Evidently the farm loan board did not take into consideration two important aspects. The first is the character of the applicant, which to my knowledge is excellent, and the second is the anticipated increase in the income of the applicant as a result of the improvements he would have been able to achieve if he had been able to obtain the loan. I have no quarrel with the idea of helping the farmers of western Canada. I heartily approve of consideration being given to improvements in the Veterans' Land Act. But Canada needs men like Mr. Klinge. Because of men like him we can now boast of the sound foundation upon which this nation is being built.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned I was speaking about the necessity of helping the small farmers. I think we should do something to improve the lot of these hardy pioneers who operate not huge wheat farms but mixed farms, dairy farms, and truck garden farms. These are the people who for the most part are the farmers in the district of Thunder Bay.
I would be remiss if I did not mention the needs of the small tourist operator, the motel owner and others who are engaged in the tourist business of our nation. They too deserve recognition in the form of assistance; not charity, but the opportunity to secure loans and to improve their holdings in order to bring more tourist dollars to Canada. They too serve this country well and are worthy of consideration along with the small businessmen.

The visit of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip for the purpose of officially opening the St. Lawrence seaway will make 1959 one of the most memorable years in the history of Canada. The sailing of the Britannia up the St. Lawrence and on to the head of the lakes, which is the end of the Canadian seaway, will undoubtedly be recorded as one of the great events of our time. The council of the city of Fort William has already appointed a reception committee, and I am informed that it is already at work in preparation for this historic event.
Day after day our newspapers carry the sad story of unemployment and its evil effects upon family life, pointing out the danger to our own way of life. This should serve as a reminder to the government of the gravity of its task. The Prime Minister has found pleasure in referring to the leader of the official opposition as a Jeremiah. I would refer the hon. gentleman to another prophet, Ezekiel, who in chapter 12, verses 22 and 24 warned us to beware of vain visions, in these words:
The days are prolonged and every vision faileth . . . for there shall be no more any vain vision nor flattering divination . . .
I respectfully submit-

Mr. Speaker, my first words are
ones of welcome and congratulation to the four new members who took their seats on opening day, January 15. At the same time I extend my deepest sympathy to the relatives and close friends of the late hon. members for Springfield and Trinity who sat with us last session. To the hon. members for Pro-vencher (Mr. Jorgenson) and Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Fortin) I offer my special congratulations, first on their having been so honoured, together with their constituencies, and second on the very excellent content and presentation of their addresses to this house.
It will be just one year at the end of this month since my predecessor for the constituency of Antigonish-Guysborough, Mr. Angus
The Address

Mr. O'Leary R. Macdonald-or "Angus D.D." as he was better known-was stricken critically ill while performing his duties in this house and as parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Transport. Mr. Macdonald somewhat miraculously survived major surgery, and though he is still very far from being a well man I am happy to be able to tell his many friends that his condition is showing constant improvement.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Hon. members have indicated that they join in extending to Mr. and Mrs. Macdonald and the family our warmest wishes for his complete recovery.
The constituency of Antigonish-Guysborough is one whose economy is based almost solely on the successful operation of three of the primary industries, namely agriculture, fishing and lumbering. The largest centre is Antigonish town itself, the home of St. Francis Xavier University, a university which has gained an international reputation in the field of adult education through its extension service. From a strictly academic point of view this university is likewise well recognized throughout this continent, and has among its present student body young men and women from every province in Canada and from many states in the United States.
The St. Francis Xavier extension department has carried on its adult education program for almost 30 years. Significant numbers of students, as individuals and as groups from the Caribbean, South America, Africa and especially from southeast Asia, have been coming for many years now to study the program of this extension department. Three of the faculty members spent some time in southeast Asia promoting the program. Two of them were taken out there by officials of the Colombo plan. One of the department's personnel spent two years in Ceylon, where he set up a little St. Francis Xavier extension department. An associate director of this department for many years was called to India three years ago to promote the program, and just last fall both he and the man who had been in Ceylon were asked to go to Australia to help out on a short course for fisheries leaders of the Asian countries from Pakistan to Japan.
On August 5, 1952, reflecting on the experience of this extension department, Dr. M. M. Coady, for many years the dynamic director of this department and now Monsignor Coady, director emeritus, outlined its fundamental philosophy in these words:
The general purpose of the St. Francis Xavier extension department was to mobilize the people for continued adult learning. This was based on the conviction that in a democracy, people should not be allowed to float down the river of events

The Address-Mr. O'Leary but that positive purposeful effort should be put In the business of bringing them along the road of progress. They should come under their own steam, of course, but it is the work of educational institutions to organize them to do this. It is also the work of educators, we believe, to spearhead the thinking of the nation. We expect this in the field of the arts and sciences; there is no reason why we should not have it also in the field of social affairs.
The fishing industry in my constituency as in many sections of Nova Scotia and the Atlantic provinces is of vital importance to our counties. In Guysborough county it is paramount. In Antigonish county it is a very significant and contributing factor to the total income of the people. True, there has been a decline in the actual number of fishermen who previously secured their entire livelihood from this source. The reasons for this are varied and fairly numerous. None the less in the past year, though the total catch was down somewhat, increased prices compensated for this drop in volume and as a result the industry, generally speaking, provided sufficient encouragement to a substantial number of our fishermen to cause them to make plans for an expanded program in the coming year, and to attract others to the industry.
A few shore sections of our counties where the residents are attempting to re-establish themselves in the industry are faced with the problem of finding proper and adequate shelter and docking facilities for their boats nearby. As the industry declined in these areas so did the facilities once placed there, which were maintained only so long as their commercial use justified the expenditure of the public moneys involved. I well realize this sane attitude on the part of the government but I do say that now, if there is any apparent hope of revitalizing the industry, no effort or expense should be spared in providing at least the essential facilities such as wharfs, breakwaters and such dredging as may be necessary to accommodate the fishermen concerned.
As for those fishing districts which have increased or maintained their volume, I must say that the Minister of Public Works has been more than sympathetic, and I wish to thank him on behalf of the fishermen of these areas for his tangible appreciation of their needs during 1957 and 1958. This does not mean that all our requirements have been met, but we are hopeful for 1959-80 and we shall continue our efforts with his office so long as our needs are in evidence and the industry continues to expand.
I believe, too, that this is the proper place to express our appreciation to the district engineer and his hard working staff in the

harbours and rivers engineering branch of the Department of Public Works at the Halifax office, for their splendid co-operation with us at all times.
About two months ago I attended the annual meetings of both the Antigonish and Guysborough federations of agriculture, and as recently as the week before last the Nova Scotia provincial federation annual meeting at Truro. I found all three meetings interesting, stimulating and encouraging. The reports and reviews of the past year's operations indicated that progress had been made, that federal and provincial government assistance to the industry contributed immeasurably toward this progress, that some problems were being solved or were capable of being solved by the farmers themselves, and that still others called for further helpful measures of assistance from government. Resolutions were presented, discussed and drafted for presentation to the appropriate bodies. Plans were made for increased production in certain types of products that could be efficiently and profitably produced and marketed. Discussion was live and frank, and as a result approved recommendations were limited to those which were of sufficient and justifiable importance as to seriously pertain to the over-all welfare of the agricultural industry.
I am happy to observe that the speech from the throne indicates that during this present session of parliament we will have an opportunity to review and revise the legislation concerning farm credit. This subject is of vital concern to my constituency and to the Atlantic provinces as a whole, as was evidenced in the resolution drafted by the Atlantic premiers' conference held in St. John's, Newfoundland, last September. A true and realistic appraisal of our family farms and a recognition of their contribution, not only to the economy of a large number of our people, but of equal and perhaps even greater significance, their contribution to the moral fibre of our society, is long past due. We maintain that our average family farm properly managed and with diversified production can provide a comfortable and enviable living for any Canadian family.
I quite agree with the statement that it requires more brains to be a successful farmer than it does to be an average member of a profession or other occupation. Speaking of Nova Scotia, I feel that we will have no difficulty in meeting this challenge because our province has a long but not proud record of exporting brains. Succeeding generations have continued to produce such men in our rural communities, and it is

these who can very successfully operate their fathers' farms and bring back into production farms that have been vacated over the past quarter century and more. But in order that our young rural people may take this, their rightful place, as proud owners and successful farmers, they must be given the opportunity to borrow the necessary funds for the many and varied improvements to be effected in their lands, buildings and farm equipment.
At the present time there is no agency that can satisfactorily serve the complete credit needs of these people. True we have farm loan boards, land settlement loans, credit unions and banks, but none of those are so constituted or equipped to serve the long term capital needs of our average small farm. It is for this reason that I see hope for our type of agriculture in that which is proposed in the throne speech with respect to farm credit.
A particular situation with respect to the operations of the unemployment insurance commission and a source of not inconsiderable inconvenience and annoyance to those in my constituency tiling claims for benefits has recently been corrected, in that we now have in the town of Antigonish for the first time our own claims agent, which service cannot help but guarantee to our people a definite improvement. Previously many delays were encountered due to improper and incomplete applications being forwarded to the office in Pictou county; and this office being over one hundred miles distant from some of the outlying districts of the constituency, it was well-nigh impossible or prohibitively costly for applicants to appear personally at this office. I wish to commend the Minister of Labour most heartily for having initiated this new improved service.
With the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) and with, I know, all hon. members of this house, I share a very deep concern over the great tragedy that struck the mining town of Springhill last October. The generous and spontaneous response of governments, organizations and individuals right across this continent genuinely demonstrated the solicitude of all. The magnitude of the disaster both in terms of lives lost and its far reaching effect upon the future of this town brought this about.
Recently we have read reports of this town's citizens being offered opportunities of employment other than at home. This effort on the part of public-spirited firms is to be admired and commended. However, when it is appreciated that the greater number of these men are no longer in their youth but are of middle age, unskilled other than as
The Address-Mr. O'Leary miners, own their own homes and have growing families, I believe anyone will agree that first every effort should be made to find employment for them at home. The government of the province of Nova Scotia has recognized the necessity for such action, and has taken the initial tangible steps for the encouragement of a local industry or industries. However, we all know that a substantial industry cannot come about overnight, so I wish to place myself on record as advocating that if this government is contemplating the erection of any type of institution in the province of Nova Scotia in the comparatively near future, which could give employment to a number of the citizens of Springhill, I strongly support the selection of this town as the site for such an institution.
At this time I will do no more than commend our government for indicating its intention to take action to alleviate the discriminatory effects of the recent horizontal increase in freight rates.
In March, 1953-and I repeat the year, 1953 *-a paper sponsored by the town council of Mulgrave and the Mulgrave board of trade entitled, a "Brief concerning the future of the town of Mulgrave" was released to governments and to the public generally. By way of introduction it read as follows:
For more than half a century the community of Mulgrave has been dependent upon the Canadian National Railway. The employment provided by the rail terminus and wharves, and the rail and road ferries connecting Cape Breton island with the mainland, have made possible the building of a pleasant and prosperous coastal town of nearly 1,200 souls.
Mulgrave is now an incorporated town with 214 residential homes, a modern school that boasts standards comparable with any in the province of Nova Scotia, three Christian churches, recreation halls and playgrounds, and all the ancillary shops and services required by a thoroughly modern and progressive rural community.
Established on a hillside overlooking the strait of Canso, Mulgrave is surrounded by rocky timbered terrain that has no agricultural possibilities. There is, however, a generous supply of seasoned timber available and a number of freshwater lakes lie in the vicinity. The deep water harbour has for centuries been a stopping place for ships plying the Atlantic seaboard; it is regarded as one of the outstanding natural harbours in the east and during the war played an important role as a naval port.
Now, after 50 years of stable growth, the community of Mulgrave faces disaster. The haunting fear of insecurity lies pregnant on the thresholds of her home. The stability of her family life is threatened; and the carefully nurtured traditions from which a lively community spirit has been fostered are in danger of fading into oblivion.
For with the construction of the Canso causeway the raison d'etre of Mulgrave's existence has come to an end. The causeway is being built from a point on the mainland at Auld Cove three miles beyond the old car and rail ferry sites, and all the activities which have provided employment to the people of the town will cease as soon as the project is completed.

The Address-Mr. O'Leary
Then, following certain proposals, the brief went on to say:
The number of men now employed by the federal and provincial governments with the Canadian National Railway and the car ferry is 288. This represents two-thirds of the total full-time working force in Mulgrave. One hundred and seventy-nine of these men have no security of tenure in their jobs and look forward to dismissal on the completion of the causeway. There are in addition, approximately 100 seasonal workers who will be affected.
Over and above this number there are 63 men now employed with the Canadian National Railway who have sufficient seniority in the company to permit their retirement or transfer to some other locality. This portion of the working force does not itself constitute a problem; but its displacement will result in a serious loss to the community.
Against this background of the working force that will be affected must be considered the social consequences that will accompany their displacement.
At a time when millions of the earth's peoples have become displaced through war, misfortune and persecution, the plight of 1,200 Canadians in the town of Mulgrave may not seem unduly grave. But we would point out that the situation which faces us was brought about not by chance but by the deliberate and planned decision of the public authorities. The people of Mulgrave did not protest the construction of the Canso causeway because it seemed the greater good of the wider community would be served by its completion. We do suggest, however, that in achieving the greater good the needs of the small number who are affected adversely by that decision cannot in justice be ignored.
One of the proposals advanced at that time was that the Canadian National Railways- and again I remind you, Mr. Speaker, this was in 1953-construct and maintain a spur line along the coast from the mainland entrance to the causeway to the town of Mulgrave. It was pointed out that without such railway connection Mulgrave could not hope to attract new industry or even hold the small industries then existing. The spur line requested would run three miles from the causeway entrance to the port.
All of the above was advanced almost six years ago, Mr. Speaker. The causeway to Cape Breton island was completed almost five years ago and the events that took place were almost identical to the predictions made a year previous, as outlined in the brief I have just read.
As recently as two weeks ago I sat down with the town's mayor, council and representatives of other interested groups and organizations, and we discussed at some length their existing problem as presented above. We arrived at the following conclusions:
One, that an engineer and economist should be sent to the strait of Canso area in an attempt to evaluate the strategic importance of this area for shipping and transshipping facilities; two, Mulgrave being the entrance to the St. Lawrence waterway and having one of the finest natural ice-free harbours on the Atlantic coast on this continent, needs this latter fact made better known to all

shipping interests. Anything that this government can do by way of publicizing this fact will be deeply appreciated. All of the facts relative to this port are easily available: 25,000-ton ships can enter this port without pilots-it is ice free the year round-during the summer it has both a north and south entrance-the harbour has a rise and fall of tide of only four feet. Every captain who has berthed his ship in this port will attest to these facts which result in a speedy and easy berthing rarely if ever found elsewhere. Three, during the winter of 1957 this port received a fair amount of freight normally handled at North Sydney. Conditions at that time resulting in the use of this port could very easily occur again. At that time all available docking facilities were utilized. As a consequence we deem it expedient that present docking facilities at Mulgrave not only be maintained but even expanded to care for present and future needs as we have good reason to believe will arise.
Four, further we believe that the Canadian National Railways spur line from the entrance to the causeway to the port of Mulgrave should be built as speedily as possible.
We in eastern Nova Scotia are very hopeful that a $40 million pulp mill will be built in the area of this port in the very near future. To date Premier Stanfield and his government have carried on successful negotiations with the company concerned; and when this pulp mill becomes a reality, that which I have recommended regarding the port of Mulgrave will be doubly necessary.
As I resume my seat, Mr. Speaker, I conclude with a general statement indicating my reaction to the speech from the throne. It is comprehensive and all-embracing and will, when its directions are implemented, have a good, positive and lasting effect on the lives of all Canadians.
