speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I want to join with previous speakers in offering my congratulations to the mover of the address, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson), and to the seconder, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin). Both hon. members performed their duties as good parliamentarians, and I am sure they have earned the admiration of their respective constituents.
I well recall in sessions gone by, when members of the present government were sitting to the left of Mr. Speaker, the comments which were made following the reading of the speech from the throne. They characterized it as an empty document, a meaningless presentation or a confused, vague concentration of generalities. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not agree with the concluding remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I have in my hand a copy of the speech now under consideration during this debate. There is no doubt in my mind that this document gains more prominence by what it does not say than by

what it contains. This document barely mentions, and in most cases completely ignores, problems which should have at this time the most careful consideration.
Last evening in this house we witnessed a demonstration by the Prime Minister who was trying to defend the speech from the throne. In the course of his remarks the Prime Minister proudly stated, and I quote from page 61 of Hansard for January 19, 1959:
-we are now moving upwards. That is, in large measure, owing to the action taken by this government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, I hear the "hear, hear". It is true that the profits of the Royal Bank of Canada moved upward in 1958, but the Prime Minister did not state what part the conversion loan of last fall played in these increased profits. Yes, we are moving upward. Figures have just been released this morning concerning unemployment in Canada which show that unemployment has been moving upward to 419,000 workers who were registered for unemployment insurance and claiming benefits in November last. We are moving upward. The cost of living is moving upward; the price index has reached an all-time high at 126.3. We are moving upward. The interest on loans to provinces and municipalities is moving upward. Everything is moving upward but the unemployed are still looking for work.
In the course of his remarks the Prime Minister also cited certain figures showing the percentage of unemployed as compared with the labour force of this country. These figures varied from 3.8 per cent in 1945 to 6 per cent in the months of February and March, 1950; 6.7 per cent for the same months in 1956; 5 per cent for comparative months in 1957. But when he came to 1958, what did the Prime Minister do? He was aware that the comparative figures for 1958 showed that unemployment had almost doubled that of any five or six years previous. When he came to 1958 he deliberately quoted the figures for the months of October and November, and it was only following pressure from this side of the house that he revealed the percentages for the months of February and March, 1958, which were up to 10 per cent, almost double that of any previous 5 or 6 years.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I realize, as does every member of this house irrespective of party, that Canada should continue to recognize the necessity for providing economic assistance to underdeveloped nations. At the last meeting in Paris on the occasion of its fourth annual conference, the NATO parliamentarians gave special and specific attention to
The Address-Mr. Robichaud the importance of technical and financial assistance to less developed areas. These matters of vital importance to NATO countries were submitted to the NATO foreign ministers' meeting in Paris last December and, without doubt, must have been considered as problems which should be given a high priority in their deliberations. The NATO countries should seek at once the means of adjusting free world economic programs to counter, and to counter effectively, the Soviet bloc economic warfare activities which are aimed at undermining the economic stability of the free world.
May I take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, of extending to you and to the other members of the Canadian parliamentary groups who attended the fourth annual conference in Paris my sincere appreciation for their cooperation and good understanding. Our visit to the Canadian air force and army centres in France and Western Germany was a revelation to all of us. The R.C.A.F. squadrons and the four Canadian infantry brigade groups are part of the international commitment on behalf of the people of Canada. Our contribution to NATO in Europe is a subject of national concern. Every Canadian should be proud of the performance of our servicemen stationed in Europe. They have a duty to perform, they have a role to play, and they are doing it to the glory of Canada in the defence of personal freedom.
But, Mr. Speaker, what do we find in the speech from the throne which could give hope, the faintest hope, for the promises made by the present government with regard to the subject of financial relations between the provinces and the dominion? Where is that new dominion-provincial conference promised for January, 1958 and shelved ever since? What has the present government done to alleviate the heavy burden of municipal taxes? Oh, I know that great publicity was given to the Prime Minister's announcement, prior to his departure for his world tour, concerning federal participation in certain municipal projects to be undertaken during the winter months. The Minister of Labour himself took glory and satisfaction in announcing that this so-called benevolent program would provide additional winter work for about 9,000 to 10,000 men.
How many municipalities are today in a position to accept this offer, at a time when the costs of construction are seriously and substantially increased as a result of the difficulties encountered during the winter months? Why was this program not instituted in September or early fall, a period when such work was practical and economical? In many cases federal assistance would

The Address-Mr. Robichaud barely cover the additional cost to the municipalities and, furthermore, the total number of workers who can benefit from this program will be just about 2 per cent of the unemployed at the present time, barely a drop in the bucket or a needle in a hay stack. This program is nothing but another example of the complete lack of foresight of the present government and its complete failure to admit the seriousness of the unemployment situation throughout the country.
Where is this grave concern of the past? Where are these bold declarations of the Prime Minister, such as that which was made in Prince Albert on February 14, 1958, when he said:
As long as I am Prime Minister, no man or woman is going to suffer from unemployment, so long as public works will provide them the assistance they require.
Then a few days later at Brantford, on February 17, 1958, here is what he said. I would ask you to listen to the words of this great evangelist, this new savior of the world:
The humblest of our people will not be forgotten. The people who are unemployed will not be in the false position of being put on relief.
Then again in Montreal on February 18 last, in a live telecast, he said:
As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada everything that can be done-everything without regard to limit-will be done to the end that no one will suffer.
Listen to what he said in Cornwall on February 24. The Conservatives had launched a winter works program and were putting forward a huge public works program to take up some of the slack in unemployment. Here are the Prime Minister's own words:
We have acted. We are meeting unemployment. We have given young Canadians the hope. We have given them the vision.
Yes, Mr. Speaker; they have given the hope and the vision, but still there is no work. What has the present speech from the throne to offer in order to take care of the situation and to implement what the Prime Minister solemnly promised with respect to unemployment? It gives more emphasis to the enactment of a bill of rights and to the approval of a statute to authorize the appointment of parliamentary secretaries who are anxious for those appointments than it does to the plea of the unemployed. What do we find in the speech from the throne? We find less than two complete lines to give hope to the unemployed. We read this:
Certain amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act will be submitted to you.
That is all we find. What does it mean? We shall wait and see, as will the unemployed. We know that the fund of over $900 million


which was available to the present government when it took office has now been depleted by probably over 50 per cent. What a difference in attitude from that of February and March, 1958 when we were on the eve of a general election; and what a surprise it must be to Canadian workers to hear a member of the present cabinet, namely the Minister of Justice, declare before a group of young Conservatives that the present unemployment situation should be blamed on the previous Liberal administration.

speechtext: That is for sure.

speechtext:
From the other side of the house I hear the interjection "That is for sure". Is the hon. member so blind and so much obsessed by the vision that he has failed to realize that his government has been in power for over 18 months? Is not the shock of the present unemployment situation serious enough to inject into his veins and into those of the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Labour and others a sense of reality and, I could add, of responsibility? If the Minister of Justice only knew how futile his arguments were on that occasion and how sterile was his achievement. I am convinced that he would react without further delay to the plea for adequate and more audacious steps to cope with the situation.
Is this the hope, the vision, that was promised in Cornwall on February 24, 1958 by the Prime Minister? For the married workers of the country, for the young and the old of Canada, is this great vision not getting dimmer and dimmer day after day and week after week? Yes, Mr. Speaker, this great vision, with its huge public works program which was supposed to provide jobs for hundreds of thousands of Canadians, has gradually vanished in less than ten months into nothing but a dream; and today we may wishfully say to the Prime Minister, "May your dreams some day come true." How desirable it would be for the Prime Minister and for his government to forget, for some time at least, about being looked upon as men of vision and to settle down to the job of running the affairs of the country.
In the present speech from the throne the plea of the unemployed has been brushed aside. It has been scuttled under the shadow of a meaningless, useless and untimely bill of rights. The right to find work is the bill of rights that the Canadian people are expecting today. If the Prime Minister and his government would give consideration to the recent pastoral letter of His Eminence Cardinal Leger, the terrific affliction of unemployment could be coped with by new and

more audacious steps to remedy this unfortunate situation. There are over 80,000 unemployed in the Montreal area alone, and from 10,000 to 15,000 young people are affected. This situation presents a problem which endangers the peace and harmony which are so essential to a sound and balanced economy.
In my own constituency of Gloucester over 7,000 persons are registered today as claimants for unemployment insurance benefits. Yes, Mr. Speaker; over 55 per cent of our labour force is registered for benefits, and even this figure does not offer a true picture of the situation. At least 2,000 more men or women have not gone to the trouble of registering with the unemployment insurance office because they knew they could not qualify, inasmuch as their eight weeks or ten weeks of contributions did not meet the requirements of the act. Proposals which I have made to the government to alleviate this deplorable condition at least in part have as yet been without result.
It does not seem fair that a farmer or his sons cannot qualify under the unemployment insurance regulations when cutting lumber or pulpwood on the family wood lots, while the same men can qualify if they leave their homes to work in lumber camps. In many cases farm owners have disposed of their wood lots at sacrifice prices to lumber or pulp dealers in order to be in a position to be rehired by these same dealers and qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. Our farmers are victims of discrimination, and an adjustment should be made in the unemployment insurance regulations in order to take care of such cases.
Requests from my constituency are at present before the Minister of Public Works for the construction of new wharves and for improvements to various harbours. Last year I expressed to the minister and to his department appreciation for their decision to proceed with major improvements to the Bathurst harbour in conjunction with mining developments contemplated for the area. Unfortunately conditions have changed. All mining activities in the area are at a standstill. Consequently the project did not materialize, and it may not take place for some years to come. The minister will admit, however, that the business interests of the Bathurst area cannot carry on much longer under present conditions. I realize that discussions are under way with the interests concerned, but I would urge the minister to give instructions to his officials to arrive at an early and favourable decision on this important problem.
The Address-Mr. Robichaud
Again, on numerous occasions I have outlined to the minister the deplorable situation of the fishermen of Maisonnette who are asking for an extension to their present wharf so that it may be used in their fishing operations. I want to repeat that the minister and the government have at Maisonnette an opportunity to provide employment to practically every available worker in the community. A practical wharf which can be constructed at a normal cost would, at the same time, provide facilities for the local fishermen and work to the shore help for at least four to six months of the year. Here the department is facing a problem which can be solved and which should receive immediate consideration.
The minister and his officials should also attempt to solve without delay the situation at Lower Caraquet. If a decision has been reached by the department, for obvious reasons, not to replace part of the present wharf recently carried away in a storm, consideration should be given to an immediate replacement. The need is urgent. A new location has been surveyed. The project is economically justified, and the local fishermen must be provided with adequate shelter and wharfage facilities for their fishing craft. I have enough confidence in the good judgment and ability of the department's engineers and other officials to expect that new construction will get under way at Lower Caraquet at least within the next few months. If no decision is reached at once in this particular case the fishermen of that community will have to wait until 1961 before they can benefit from wharfage facilities and operate with efficiency. It will mean more unemployment, more suffering for the people of this fishing community.
I also understand that the reconstruction and improvement of the Shippegan wharf have received the approval of the minister and his department. Shippegan is one of the largest fishing ports on the Atlantic coast, and it is urgent that the improvement asked for be undertaken without further delay.
The survey now under way by the public works department to provide shelter for the 50-odd fishing boats at Pigeon Hill should also be given priority. The fishermen concerned are awaiting with anxiety the announcement of the department's decision in this regard. The Minister of Public Works must be aware that the construction of public buildings must not necessarily get top priority on his advanced list of projects. The construction of a wharf or improvement of a harbour will not only provide work in the

The Address-Mr. Robichaud construction period but will provide additional facilities to expand such industries as fishing, shipping and others.
In my constituency we have a difficult problem with regard to the improvement of Tracadie harbour. This is a matter which should also receive top priority on the list of advanced planning projects to be undertaken by the department. Improved harbour conditions at Tracadie would provide facilities leading to the establishment of a substantial fishing industry so urgently needed in Tracadie and adjoining communities.
On May 19 last, Mr. Speaker, while speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I brought to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue and the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the plea of over a quarter of a million of our population in northern New Brunswick and the Gaspe peninsula who are deprived of practically any television reception or service. Eight months have gone by and our people are no better off today, no further ahead than they were in May of last year. I understand that permission has been granted for the establishment of a privately owned television station at New Carlisle which would serve part of the area concerned with programs 35 per cent in English and 65 per cent in French. This station was supposed to be in operation in August, 1958, but due to unforeseen difficulties it was announced that its operation would be delayed to a later date last fall. A further delay has since taken place, and we are now told that we will have to wait until the fall of 1959 before the inauguration of this television service.
Very little has been accomplished so far toward the realization of this project, and our entire population is showing its dissatisfaction. The proposed service, consisting of 35 per cent English and 65 per cent French programs, will not be satisfactory to our population. Such a service has been tried elsewhere. It has been tried right here in Ottawa and has proven most impractical and unsatisfactory. What our population want-I said it last year and I repeat it-are the same service and the same privileges which are offered today to other populated areas of Canada.
Attempts have been made to misinform our population by telling them that it is impossible for the C.B.C. to extend to our area the service or the facilities of the English television network, for the only reason that the nearest television station at Moncton is privately owned. This is not altogether so, Mr. Speaker, and the people of Gloucester county and northeastern New Brunswick should be made aware of the true facts in

this regard. It is true that the Moncton station is a privately owned station, but this does not prevent the C.B.C. from establishing relay stations or microwave towers which could be attached to the English network passing through Edmundston and then extending to Moncton, Halifax and Sydney.
The people of Gloucester county and of northern New Brunswick are Canadian taxpayers who are contributing their share for the operation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Our people have a right to enjoy and to share with their fellow Canadians in their own living rooms a community of interest, and to participate in events of national importance. Why should such a concentration of population be prevented from enjoying on television such instantaneous visual communications as the opening of the Canadian parliament or the important events of Her Majesty's visit to Canada next summer?
All across Canada microwave towers are going up. The Rocky mountains have been spanned and a link has been completed with Canada's newest province, Newfoundland. Yet the residents of Gloucester county, as well as other residents of a largely populated area in northern New Brunswick and the Gaspe coast, are still deprived of participation in the national television system. Again I want to emphasize that the proposed station at New Carlisle, if it ever materializes, will not be satisfactory to a large proportion of our population. It will not be satisfactory to the 12,000 residents of the Bathurst area and to other communities in my constituency and adjoining counties.
It could be difficult to give adequate service to certain remote areas because of excessive costs, but anyone familiar with the present television networks will soon realize that the connections extending through Edmundston and Moncton could easily and reasonably be extended to cover Campbell-ton in Restigouche and Bathurst in Gloucester county. Such a service is justified by the large concentration of population it would cover, and more so by the absence of technological difficulties which have been encountered in other sections of the country.
We hear these days of meetings in the prairie provinces to organize a march on Ottawa by the western grain producers, fighting for deficiency payments on wheat. If we have a wheat cry in the west, we also have a cry for television service in northeastern New Brunswick. Our people are alarmed. Petitions have been circulated, letters have been sent to the minister and to the C.B.C., and what we want now is something better than consideration or study. We want action, and we want action now. I sincerely hope that the Minister of National

Revenue, who has done so well in this particular field for his own communities in Nova Scotia, will without further hesitation transmit to the C.B.C. with his recommendation the plea of the dissatisfied population of northern New Brunswick. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I sincerely hope that on January 1, I960, next New Year's day, my constituents will have the opportunity to hear and share with their fellow Canadians through their television sets the New Year's message of our Prime Minister.
Mr. Pallet!: And for many years to come.

speechtext:
Well, they have to hear it next year because if we wait too long they will not be in a position to hear it at all. When well over 85 per cent of the Canadian population is within reach of good television service, and when over 75 per cent of Canadian households have acquired television sets, it does not seem fair that we in Gloucester county and northern New Brunswick should be prevented from sharing in what has been called the most rapid development of television service in any country in the world.
The time allotted to me will not allow me to discuss freely in the course of the present debate a matter of major importance to most of the fishing communities in the maritimes. It has to do with the serious situation developing in the administration of lobster fishery regulations in the maritime provinces, and particularly in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. I take no exception to the decision of the minister and the department to prosecute, to use the minister's own words, "as vigorously as the law requires" anyone catching or canning lobster illegally. The minister is threatening poachers with stiff penalties, and most unfortunate incidents could follow unless his department at once, without delay, takes a different view of this most serious problem.
Since my first speech in the house I have at every session urged the department to alter its policy toward illegal lobster fishing.
I have repeated again and again that more good could be accomplished by a fishery officer by a friendly chat with the fishermen at the end of a wharf or even at the corner store than by determination to play this game of "hide and seek" in order to catch a fisherman committing the offence of illegal fishing.
I am again warning the Minister of Fisheries that the only means of curbing this illegal practice is through education. If the minister would divert less than 10 per cent of his department's estimates for the protection branch alone, and use it towards the education of the fishermen, I can assure him that his problem would be solved in a very short period. If the minister would divert 1 per 66968-9-7i
The Address-Mr. Robichaud cent of the protection branch estimate toward the education of the lobster fishermen alone, his problem would be solved. Otherwise if he insists on this rough and tough practice I warn him again that he is looking for more trouble. This Cuban method cannot be allowed in this country, and unless a drastic and effective system of education is introduced at once the minister and his department will be held responsible for the consequences. I will be back on this subject at a later date.
From recent reports which have reached us the coal industry in the maritimes and particularly in Nova Scotia is suffering a depression as serious as the one which it had to face in the spring and summer of last year. Here again we find that the government shows uncertainty and inconsistency in dealing with the problem. On Friday last, as reported on page 11 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys the following very simple question:
My question is based on a news dispatch in today's Montreal Gazette announcing the intended closing on February 1 of five collieries affecting 4,000 men-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext: Order. I think I recall the hon. member reading that earlier today. Could he not trust the memory of the house, without repeating the whole quotation?

speechtext:
I will endeavour to respect your views, Mr. Speaker.
The minister clearly stated at that time that he did not receive any notice from the Dosco company with regard to a cutdown in production or a staff reduction. When, with a telegram in my hand, I asked the minister a second question-whether any protest or representations had been made by local unions of the united mineworkers of America, I received an altogether different reply. Hon. members may recall that in his answer, as printed on page 12 of Hansard, the minister said:
Their representatives came and met with us some time ago. They did make representations, and I must add that the matter is now under consideration and that we propose to come to a decision in regard to this in the near future.
What a contradiction in the two replies of the minister. At first, he declared he had no knowledge of the situation. A few moments later he told us that representations along that line and in connection with other matters were made to the government by the Dosco company. The company's representatives, he said, had met with the government some time ago. At first, he had no knowledge of the matter; next, that they had made

The Address-Mr. Robichaud representations and the matter was under consideration. What a contradiction. It is a confusion which is typical of the government's actions today.
If we go back to the coal debate which took place on July 1 of last year we find that we were told by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), as reported on page 1801 of Hansard of July 1, 1958, that orders were on hand for 4,600,000 tons of coal and that following the five or six weeks shutdown contemplated at that time the crisis in the coal industry would be over. The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys stated at that time that orders were on hand for the entire stockpile and that the company was only waiting transportation. Six months later we are meeting the same situation, a situation which is extremely unsatisfactory to the 9,000 or 10,000 coal miners of the maritime provinces.
Something is just not right in the coal industry, and I challenge the government to take the matter in hand and take action at once to remedy the situation. It does not seem logical that with a stockpile of 1,200,000 tons of coal in Cape Breton there should have been this winter such a shortage of domestic coal in the maritime provinces. It does not seem logical that, under such circumstances American coal should have been imported into Moncton and other centres of New Brunswick. In my own constituency of Gloucester there were shortages of domestic coal in December and early January. This does not seem fair to the coal miners who are being laid off in Nova Scotia, and to the miners of the Minto coal fields in New Brunswick, who were cut down to two or three days of work per week in the last four of five months.
Are the coal companies really making an effort to sell coal as they should do? Action by the government should be taken now before the lay-off of February 1 takes place. It is the responsibility of the government to get the true facts, to get a true picture of the situation in order to give adequate protection to the miners concerned and to make factual reports to parliament and to the country.
Unfortunately I do not have time this afternoon to discuss this matter in as full detail as I should like to do. It is the responsibility of the government to cope with the situation even if this means granting an additional subsidy to the industry. If our miners are allowed to work, the additional expenditure involved would be repaid time and time again by its benefits to the Canadian economy. Otherwise there will again be a merciless curtailment of employment in the coal fields and it is the duty of the government to

prevent such a curtailment and such contemplated lay-offs. It is also the responsibility of the government to find ways and means of coping with the situation. They have accepted the responsibility of power, and on them lies the responsibility of action.
There are other matters to which I should like to call the attention of the government, but further occasions and opportunities will be offered to us in the course of the present session. The question of freight rates is vital to the economy of the Atlantic provinces and we will have an opportunity to deal thoroughly with this problem at a later date. The people of the Atlantic provinces are aware that the pledges made by the 32 Tory candidates prior to the election have, to a major extent, been ignored. What about such pledges as those in connection with defence contract expenditures in the Atlantic provinces; the establishment of crown corporations in the Atlantic provinces; and special fiscal considerations to encourage the establishment of industries in the Atlantic provinces? I ask hon. gentlemen opposite how much money has been spent by the federal government out of items which have been included for the last two years in the estimates of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources for the construction of the East Saint John thermal plant. Not yet a single penny, I am informed.
These are matters which we intend to bring to the attention of the house and of the country during the course of this session of parliament and for which the government will be asked to answer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I should like to express my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address. I should like to say to the hon. member for Provencher-and I say this as a member who does not represent a rural or agricultural constituency-that I found his speech on agriculture made more sense to me than any other speech on this subject I have heard in this chamber.
To the seconder, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet, may I say that the charm of the delivery of his broadly humanitarian speech reminded me of certain occasions in my extreme youth when I had the great pleasure of hearing political speakers from the province of Quebec when they were in my part of the country. They were Liberals, it is true, but they were big shots or big leaguers. Today that party only seems capable of producing bee-bees.
If I may be permitted to do so I should also like at the outset of my remarks to say to you, Mr. Speaker, how glad I am that you occupy the chair of this house.

I wish to to speak briefly today about the province of British Columbia, the Pacific province, and I refer to it as such for this reason. In Canada there is sometimes a little confusion caused by the broad term "the western provinces" or "the west". I think I am correct, both according to history and tradition, when I say that in Canada when the west has been spoken of, or even earlier when reference was made to the great northwest, the meaning intended was that area which now comprises the prairie provinces. British Columbia is the Pacific province. I would like to explode for all time any remnants that may exist in the minds of anyone of the myth about there being a barrier between British Columbia and the rest of Canada because of the Rocky mountains. I have even had people ask me what sort of people lived west of the Rocky mountains. I have been asked, "Are the people there more like Americans?" That kind of thinking has resulted from the old myth about the mountains being a barrier.
All Canadians, including the people of British Columbia, are proud of our national motto that Canada is a nation from sea to sea. We love the words of the poet that are engraved in stone above the door of the main entrance of this building in which this chamber is housed. I refer to the words of the poet:
The wholesome sea is at her gates, her gates both east and west.
I wish to deal for a little time with the western gate of Canada. On that day in 1867 when British North America became the Dominion of Canada those words of the poet would not have been applicable because a barrier did exist as a result of the Rocky mountains. West of the mountains lay the crown colony of British Columbia which had recently fused with the colony of Vancouver island in 1866. Following confederation in 1867 the legislature of the crown colony of British Columbia took up an important debate. I was taught in school that the question in issue in this debate was whether or not they would remain a crown colony or join Canada. When I grew older and became a law student I had the opportunity of reading the verbatim record of those debates. To my amazement and somewhat to my horror I learned that although these venerable old gentlemen did discuss the question of joining Canada they also discussed whether or not British Columbia would join the United States in preference to joining Canada. Thank goodness the result has been what it was. British Columbia did
The Address-Mr. McPhillips join confederation in 1871. The Rocky mountains ceased to be any sort of barrier and the province became the greatest junction in the nation.
I shall not deal in detail with all the terms of union but under one of those terms the transcontinental railway was built under the vision of Sir John A. Macdonald and Canada became a nation extending from sea to sea with a national railway transportation system.
I should like to read from a recent article by Gus Sivertz which appeared in the good old Liberal Victoria Times in November 1958. Dealing with a statement made by a highly distinguished visitor to that area he said:
But for this momentous decision on the part of British Columbia to remain British, and to unite with the almost unkown Canadians far away to the east . . . the Canadian nation of today would have been impossible, even unthinkable!"
The province expanded and under the policies of Sir John A. Macdonald which had nation-wide application it prospered in those early days. He had great regard for the west coast and its importance. In fact at one time he was a candidate in the riding which I now have the honour to represent. I have in my hand a statement taken from the Victoria Colonist of October 22, 1878. This paper is the oldest continuously published daily newspaper on the entire Pacific coast and celebrated its hundredth anniversary on December 11. On that date it had published a newspaper every day for a hundred years which is probably a record for more than the Pacific coast. The article to which I referred is entitled, "City Elects John A." and as I said it is dated October 22, 1878. It reads as follows:
The election of representatives for the House of Commons for Victoria district took place yesterday and resulted in the return of Sir John A. Macdonald at the head of the poll-and also the election of Mr. Amor de Cosmos.
Shortly after the result of the election was declared a number of persons congregated at the corner of Government and Yates, where a cord of wood was deposited and ignited.
Of course, the Liberal government came into office in Canada in 1896.

speechtext: What about 1958?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I shall deal with 1958 later. At the moment I am referring to 1896 at which time the Liberal government came into office and the Pacific province was assigned a back seat in the affairs of the nation because that particular party had not been very interested in British Columbia and its inception, confederation or anything else. However, we were lucky in that we had a

The Address-Mr. McPhillips strong provincial administration under a gentleman who was later to become Sir Richard McBride and that Conservative government came into power in 1903 and remained in office until 1916. He was probably the greatest premier British Columbia ever had and so the province progressed internally.
In 1911 the Conservative government of Sir Robert Borden came into power and British Columbia came into its own again. Great improvements were made in the harbours of Vancouver and Victoria among other things and I shall deal later with these harbours and particularly that of Victoria. After careful consideration the Borden government decided to enlarge the outer harbour of Victoria to approximately three times its size. They built two magnificent ocean docks at Ogden Point and a large sum of money was expended for this purpose. That government also built a breakwater to protect the docks on the side from which the worst storms arose. Another breakwater was promised but unfortunately world war I came along and as we know that war brought in its wake a period of depression and nothing further could be done during those years.
In the harbour of Vancouver the Borden government built the great Ballantyne pier, which was recognized at that time to be the finest ocean pier in the entire world, and the first foundation upon which the great grain elevators in Vancouver were constructed, with the result that the golden harvest of the prairies could come to the west for the first time and find a storage place.
A little later, after the first world war, we were lucky in having as the federal representative from Victoria, Dr. Simon Fraser Tolmie, who afterwards became the premier of the province. Toward the end he was the minister of agriculture in the Borden administration and he was also in the Meighen government. Dr. Tolmie decided that the promise of the Borden government of those outer harbour installations in Victoria would be implemented. He had another idea also, namely, that the west coast of Canada should have the biggest drydock in the world. The government could not afford both and he was given his choice. Very wisely he chose the drydock, and that drydock was built as a Conservative project. It was the biggest dry-dock in the world at that time and it is still one of the biggest. It has brought great prestige to Canada as a maritime nation; it has brought millions of dollars worth of work to the west coast and it has been responsible for millions of dollars in wages to Canadian workmen.

Incidentally, it is remembered by many people that during the last war, after Singapore had gone to glory, it was the only other drydock on the Pacific ocean that could handle the great ship the Queen Elizabeth, the largest vessel in the entire world. This great ship had to come all the way into the north Pacific to reach our drydock on the west coast, which providentially was there. It handled that vessel, although the superintendent told me that when she was in the dock there were only six inches to spare on either side and 10 feet forward and 10 feet aft. The Canadian shipwrights and artisans clambered on board and they converted that great ship from a luxury passenger liner to a troop and ammunition ship. On her first trip as a troopship she actually carried 10,000 troops to the south Pacific in connection with the war with Japan.
Then the government of Mr. William Lyon Mackenzie King came into power, and again the Pacific province received a body blow. Mr. King and his Liberals were not interested in continuing the project of the Borden government, oh, no! The outer harbour of Victoria remained without its second breakwater, the Macaulay point breakwater. I suggest to this government that the time has come for the promise to be fulfilled and for the outer harbour of Victoria to receive the extra protection of the Macaulay point breakwater so as to render the harbour perfectly safe for the big vessels which come in there and encourage more vessels to come in because, believe me, Mr. Speaker, some of the pilots are in quite a nervous state when they have large vessels under control. They have to go so slowly that they almost lose steerage way. If there is a slop from the southwest it is a mighty tricky business.
I wish to say something with regard to the docks themselves. What did the Mackenzie King government do? They took them out of the management of the Department of Public Works in 1923 and gave them over to the Canadian National Railways. Ever since then the Canadian National Railways have allowed them to deteriorate and now the sheds, along with those magnifieient ocean docks, are in a state of dilapidation as a result of the maladministration by the Canadian National Railways.
While I am on this subject, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say this. It is not entirely related but it has to do more with the management of this great company. What about the great Queen Elizabeth hotel in the city of Montreal which cost the people of Canada over $27 million; not the city of Montreal or the province of Quebec but the Canadian people? What do we find? I think

the Canadian people are generous enough and sporting enough to pay for that hotel and have it receive the benefit of being part of a chain of railway hotels across this country such as the Chateau Frontenac in Quebec city, the Chateau Laurier in Ottawa, the Macdonald in Edmonton and, of course, that gem, the Chateau Lake Louise in the rocky mountains. I am sure the Canadian people would have been happy if that great hotel had received the name of an early and great Canadian. That hotel should have been called the Chateau Maisonneuve. But the name it received, Mr. Speaker, was not chosen; it was dictated. What did we find when the cat came out of the bag? Yes, the big tom cat came out of the bag. We found that this $27 million gem of hotel construction, which was built by the people of Canada, was given away by the management of the C.N.R. and made an integral part of the hotel empire of Conrad Hilton. This is another illustration of the way the Canadian National Railways operate. I will have a little more to say on this point when I reach it.
They tell me that Conrad Hilton is looking for a hotel site in the city of Vancouver. I suppose he is looking for a group of people of the type that Barnum said was born every minute, but I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that with the present administration in office we need to worry that the Canadian National Railways are going to pull that stunt again through Conrad Hilton.
Actually, this is not what I rose to say. I wanted to deal with another phase of the facilities in the port of Victoria. I now refer to the inner harbour. At one time there was a very fine dock in our harbour of Victoria, a government dock built first by the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and then taken over, of course, by the Canadian National Railways. Those wharves were right downtown because our harbour is in the heart of the city. The Canadian Pacific railway docks were on one side and the Canadian National Railways on the other. The Canadian National Railways did not run so many ships, with the result that ferries and other vessels coming from Seattle or Port Angelus could dock at the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian Pacific railway did not want them at their docks. They could dock at the Canadian National Railways for a nominal and proper dockage fee.
What happened? In 1947 a change took place, and a sand, gravel and cement company brought their cement mixers and machinery on to this dock site and the business people of Victoria believed that the Canadian National Railways had leased out those docks. But that was not the case, because it developed that the Canadian National Railways
The Address-Mr. McPhillips had sold that asset of the Canadian people in the inner harbour of the port of Victoria. Now, of course, it is no longer available to other vessels, and it is a very awkward matter for the transportation system in to that port. Because we had a government-owned dock all those years we should still have it. I ask the present government to replace that dock and that we have facilities again where ships can come and pay reasonable dockage charges.
But this is only part of the story. This is the part that I really want to draw attention to, Mr. Speaker. We have never been able to find out how much money the Canadian National got for these docks because this big pooh-bah down in Montreal says he will not tell anybody. He sold an asset of the Canadian people, but he will not say how much he got for it. The first session I was here I put a question on the order paper and got an answer. They said the date of sale was 1947, and that it was sold to Evans, Coleman & Johnson Brothers. However, the answer I really wanted does not appear. I was told it is not the policy of this company to give this sort of information.

speechtext: Ask the minister. He is a member of your own party.

speechtext:
I know who I am going to ask. I am going to ask that fellow I mentioned before by description when he comes down to the committee, and I shall wring the answer out of him, do not worry.
The amazing thing is that in 1947 the city of Victoria was represented by a cabinet minister in the Liberal administration, and an important one, too. He was such a palace favourite that he afterwards became ambassador to Japan. Apparently he could not obtain this information, or would not. In any event, such entities as the chamber of commerce of Victoria and so forth still do not know how much was paid for these wharves. In any event, we shall find that out. In the meantime, I should like to urge this government to replace them because they never should have been sold and the port of Victoria is suffering because they were.
There are some people who will say, after all, the port of Victoria is not one of the great ports of Canada. I am just going to give you some figures on that aspect of the matter. It is not as important, of course, as the port of Vancouver or Montreal, but I have here a clipping from the Victoria Colonist of December 31, 1958 containing a statement by the harbour master of the port of Victoria. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, this is a good answer or one of the many good answers to those dispensers of gloom yesterday in regard to the economy of Canada.

The Address-Mr. McPhillips This is the heading: "One of Our Best Years: 301 Deep-Sea Ships Use Docks in 1958". The article reads:
Victoria's outer wharf is drawing to the close of one of its best-ever years for deep-sea traffic-and there is no reason why 1959 can't be that much better.
Capt. Ronald Newell, harbour master, said yesterday that by midnight tonight 301 deep-sea ships would have used the outer docks, discharging and taking on cargo.
The vessels that come to the port of Victoria are all big ones. They are about 10,000 tons or over, so simple multiplication shows that we had about 3 million tons of shipping, which is about one-half of the amount for Vancouver. The large ports on the Pacific coast are Vancouver, Seattle and San Francisco. Vancouver reported about 6 million, Seattle about 11 million and San Francisco was up around 42 million; that is a lot of shipping.
The article goes on to say:
Incoming ships bring a great variety of goods for use and consumption in Victoria.
These include cars direct from the old country; liquor and wine from Britain and from 'down under'; Japanese oranges from the Orient; quantities of naval supplies; many food items from Britain and the United States; meat and wool from Australia and New Zealand; steel for the shipyards.
The deep-sea vessels leave Victoria heavily laden with lumber and grain. Exact figures for shipments of these exports were not available yesterday, but grain exports were substantially up from 1957 and lumber shipments almost 25 per cent above the previous year's total.
All this activity was achieved despite a five-week longshoremen's strike which idled the docks for that period.
There again we have a contradiction of the kind of gloom that was dispensed here yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). Incidentally, when he undertook to say that there were dirty dishes in the governmental sink, I should like to inform him that that is not so. However, when this government took office there were dirty dishes in the sink, and furthermore there was no soap.

speechtext: You did not wash them. They are still dirty, if they were at that time.

speechtext:
I should like now to deal with another question entirely, and to make another recommendation to the government. Because of the beauty of the southern tip of Vancouver island, and because of the salubrious climate which makes it unnecessary to buy much fuel to keep warm in winter, this area is a haven for retired people. I have many of them in my riding who are living on pensions. The question with which I am going to deal now is the payment of the old age pension outside of Canada. I cannot see any reason whatever, particularly since the pension is on a contributory basis

now and has been for some years, why Canada should not pay the pension outside of this country if the pensioner desires it.
We have the best of precedents for that course. This action has been taken by Great Britain, by the United States of America, by Australia and by New Zealand. This is only a humanitarian proposition. There would be only a very few such pensioners and there would only be a trickle of dollars going outside the country when compared to the total amount paid. I have so often seen this rule work hardship. You may have an old couple who have lived their lives in this country, been good citizens, paid their taxes, and then when they are old they find their family has been dispersed. The only people in the world whom they have may be a brother or a sister in Scotland, England or France and these pensioners cannot go there. I think this is entirely wrong, and I recommend to the government that the act be amended accordingly.
I would not be dealing with Pacific problems properly if I did not say something about the activities of our premier, this sawdust Caesar who struts around the province of British Columbia like a barnyard rooster talking about the expenditure of millions and millions of dollars. We have a very serious situation there now, and that is the great giveaway to the Wenner-Gren interests in respect to the power on the Peace river. He may have fooled some, but he did not fool me with all this talk about mineral claims, and this and that. No, it was the Peace river water power that they wanted. Now, he says, we have not given away anything; I have not given away a teaspoonful of water-not yet. What he has done is this. He has put a reserve on that water and that land and only allowed this outfit to go in and make surveys.
You know what is going to happen when the surveys are completed and they want to use it. No one else will be able to get it because this organization has it under reserve. There is just one hope for stopping this terrible giveaway, this terrible steal in the province of British Columbia, and that is action by the parliament of Canada. The Peace river crosses the provincial boundary and flows into Alberta. This fact gives us a toehold to stop him; under existing legislation we have something to say about it. I have every confidence that my government will take the proper steps in that connection.
I have requested certain things for British Columbia. I came here as a Canadian first, a British Columbian second, and a Victorian third. But the things I have pressed for are

Canadian. The most westerly port of Canada must be a proper port in every respect. The west coast of Canada is every bit as important as is the east coast. I should like to suggest to this government that they might take a little bit longer look at the western Arctic. There is plenty being done in connection with the eastern Arctic. However, the western Arctic happens to be a great deal closer to the U.S.S.R. than is the Atlantic Arctic. I deprecate it when I hear Canadians indulging in such phrases as "When Russia attacks", "If we have a war with Russia", and "If and when Russia attacks". I do not believe in that sort of thing. I think it is war mongering. It is not good. Nevertheless, let us be realistic. There are places on the Bering strait where you could almost come across from the U.S.S.R. in a rowboat as the area is so narrow. I would commend to the government that more attention be paid to the western Arctic in all respects.
I have just about exhausted my time. I find it most edifying to be here and to be a supporter of this government. My support of the right hon. gentleman who occupies the chair of the Prime Minister in this chamber goes back a long way. I was just looking at the smiling face of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker) this morning and remembering the time when, away back in 1942, he and I were two on the team-a very small team it was; a corporal's guard you might say-and we supported that gentleman in his first run for the leadership of the party in Winnipeg in 1942. Our horse did not win but we ran again. We were back in Ottawa in 1948. But then we had a general in charge in the person of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes). We lost again.
In those conflicts that group was obliged to take a certain amount of laughter from some of the big wheels in the party and the odd sneer and jeer. One does not like that sort of thing. I do not like to be laughed at. I do not know whether or not some people like it. However, there is an old saying that he who laughs last, laughs best. When the objective was accomplished years later I must say that I did not feel like laughing. Rather I felt edified. I felt that we had accomplished the thing that Canada needed.
As I said before, we are here as Canadians first. If I do not get for my port these things from the Minister of Public Works, at least I will feel that as a Canadian, over those years I have mentioned, I have been in some small but persistent part responsible for placing at the Prime Minister's desk in this chamber the greatest Canadian of all time.
The Address-Mr. Regier

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. McPhillips) I may say at the outset that at one time many long years ago-I believe it was 21 years ago now-I also thought that the hon. member for Prince Albert had considerable ability as a leader and that some day he ought to go far. I must say that it was about 21 years ago that I changed my mind about the abilities of that man to occupy the post of Prime Minister of Canada. I am hoping that the day will yet arrive when the people of Victoria will have a representative who will come to the same conclusion as that to which I came away back in 1938.
I am sure that the people of Victoria who were unemployed last December 31-and there were 4,981 of them, according to the figures of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) -do not have very much to do. They will therefore, without a doubt, take a great deal of pleasure in reading the remarks their member has just made on their behalf in this House of Commons. He reviewed for them some of the history of the province of British Columbia. He castigated the activities of the Mackenzie King government. He complained about the management of the C.N.R. in regard to the new hotel in the city of Montreal. He complained of the rate of fees that ships are obliged to pay when they come to Victoria. I am sure they will somehow be a little bit more brilliant than am I and that they will be able to see how that will help supply them with employment so that they might meet their grocery bills at the end of this month.
Like millions of other Canadians, now that we have returned to what may be called a normal session of parliament, I had expected to see a sincere effort on the part of the government of Canada to meet the needs of the nation. I must express my great disappointment at the absence of progressive, forward looking and aggressive measures in the speech from the throne. I fail to find them. The needs of the people of Canada are great. There is an area of uncertainty that obtains in all walks of life. The millionaire is almost as worried as are the unemployed. Most of us Canadians were looking to this session for some measures to be undertaken that would assure a little bit of stability to the Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, opposition members are often misunderstood both by members who support the government and by the electorate at large. We have in this House of Commons a responsibility that members on the government side may not have. There are eight
106	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Regier of us in this group compared with 208 on the government side. There are all kinds of members of parliament whose responsibility, without a doubt, is to tell the people of Canada what wonderful things the government has in mind for them. It is our responsibility to tell the people of Canada of the failings and the shortcomings of the government of Canada. One thing that we intend to do not only this year but in the years to come is to keep on reminding this government of the promises they made in order to obtain the confidence of the Canadian electorate. I think members of this house must agree that that is one of the responsibilities of the opposition.
I am not one who will fail to acknowledge that many good things have been done by this government as well as by former governments. This is my government exactly as it is the government of every other Canadian, and I accept it as such. However, Mr. Speaker, I am not willing to lose my speech in my efforts to become bilingual or to wrap myself in the old flag or some version of a new flag or to have my mind taken away from the needs of the day by some northern mirage or vision. I believe there are urgent problems facing the Canadian people at this time, problems that should be met at a normal session of parliament when political considerations ought to recede into the background. These urgent national problems are not being met by what is contained in the speech from the throne that has been presented to us.
I should like to go a little further afield than our national problems for a moment, Mr. Speaker, because yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) did so. Yesterday my house leader listed the urgent national problems. However, I want to say that we in the western world are facing a decision that we must make. Unless we are willing to plan our own economy and integrate it with the economies of all the other nations of the western or so-called free world we cannot hope to survive in the battle to which the Prime Minister referred yesterday. The well organized, well planned, well integrated nation to nation plan of the communist world is going to win the cold war unless the western world wakes up and decides that we can no longer carry on under the economic anarchy that many of us choose to call free enterprise. We must tighten our belts and buckle on our armour. We must convince the world that people under liberty, freedom and democracy are able to do more than people under a totalitarian regime. We pay a ridiculous lip service to a free enterprise that has long ago ceased to exist, that is


nothing but a wonderful name for economic anarchy which is going to lead us as a nation to a state of chaos and which will lead the western world into losing the battle against the more highly organized and more ruthless totalitarian regime that exists in the world today.
Most of the western world realizes the necessity for taking action. Look at what the nations of western Europe are now doing in forming a common market. But we in Canada and our friends south of the border, and I regret to say that latterly we have made efforts to pull the people of the United Kingdom down with us, think that we can afford the luxury of letting every interest within our borders carry on in its own merry, sweet and selfish way without regard to the effect on our whole way of life and on our society. At this time I should like to read a few words of warning, as found in the Toronto Telegram of August 23 last, that were sounded by Cardinal McGuigan of the city of Toronto when he said:
Perhaps one of the most widely known of all forms of this un-Christian political theory is economic nationalism which often results in waves of propaganda piling up a spirit of insularity, of national hyperconsciousness, of antagonism toward neighbour nations, and excessive tariffs-
I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) is listening. I continue:
-embargoes and exchange restrictions backing up in practical form a buy-at-home advertising barrage.
I hope the Canadian Chamber of Commerce is listening. I continue:
Once this tendency to build up nationalism and restrict world trade develops, we note the inevitable consequences of aggression (or defence) for economic reasons and increased poverty and unemployment.
I hope that the people responsible for the government of Canada will think over very carefully the warning sounded by the cardinal in that article. Before I left home we had what we call a legislators' advisory conference. There were other conferences held, and from the hundreds of representations recently made to me I find that our problems are very much the same as when I first entered the House of Commons five years ago, the only difference being that some of them are more acute today than they were at that time. These problems have not been met. One of the favourite reasons put forward by former governments and the present government for not meeting these problems is that we have to spend so much of government revenue to defend ourselves against possible communist aggression.
I have with me a photograph which appeared in the Vancouver Sun on Wednesday, December 17 last. It shows a man sleeping

on a parking lot. For a mattress he has newspapers and for a blanket he has more newspapers. I think it is about time that we took another look at our so-called defence expenditures which now total $1,700 million a year because not attending to the needs of this unemployed man, not attending to the needs of many others like him in Canada, will do more to bring communism than anything the master minds in the kremlin may devise.
I wish to return to the election pledges of the government. I know that they have kept some and may keep others. We are told that some form of crop insurance and a roads to resources program can be expected. We are told that we can expect some action to alleviate discrimination in freight rates and that we can expect more farm credit legislation. I have also noticed in the newspapers that the city of Prince Albert can expect the government to share the cost of a new bridge across the river. I should like to sound a note of warning to the government. I am very happy to read that the government is prepared to share the cost of a bridge in the city of Prince Albert but may I ask this question? Is it a navigable river or will the bridge join two provinces? If the city of Prince Albert is entitled to this, then people in many other parts of Canada have an equal right to ask the government to share the cost of a bridge that may be necessary in their own area.
I have before me a book of election promises of the Prime Minister, other ministers of the cabinet and supporters of the Conservative party. I am only going to refer to the election pledges in the 1958 campaign, although I have with me a much heavier volume containing the election pledges of the 1957 campaign. However, the 1958 book says, among other things, that all the pledges given in 1957 are valid and will be honoured. I have not bothered to look through Hansard in order to refer to all the other promises made on the floor of the house in the past five or six years. However, I believe that the people of Canada have a right to expect the government to show that it takes something more than simply a Machiavelian approach to its election promises and that the government should supply some signs that it intends to honour its election pledges. I am sure if the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) or the hon. member for York East (Mr. McGregor), or the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) had been leading the Conservative party, 10 per cent of those pledges would have been more than adequate for them and for their sense of responsibility; but we had such a vast array that it is not surprising that from the 1958 66968-9-
The Address-Mr. Regier campaign I was able to find over half a hundred election promises which so far I have seen no attempt to meet.
First of all, agriculture was assured that floor prices would bear a fair relationship to the cost of production. The pulpwood farmers were assured that pulpwood would be given a floor price; potato farmers were assured that their commodity would be given a floor price; and farmers as a whole were assured that no Canadian farmer would be allowed to suffer because of the dumping of agricultural products by the United States. Those who think there is too much spread between the price the farmer receives and the price the consumer has to pay were assured-and I am using the words given in the paper-that this "layer of fat" would be trimmed so that the farmer would receive more. Western farmers were assured that the making of deficiency payments would receive some consideration, unless our newspapers are wrong. The Montreal Star of March 17 reported a meeting held in Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan on March 15 and the quotation is ascribed to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister now says he never gave this assurance; we have to take his word for it, and I do. However, many farmers were under the impression that deficiency payments would receive serious consideration.
I should like to refer now to the vision and to other election pledges which have not been kept and with regard to which there is very little sign that they will ever be kept. There was the promise of an Arctic research program and the development of Arctic sea routes; we were promised that there would be increased self government for the Northwest Territories; it was said we had to speed up development of our Arctic resources because by 1988 Canada's population would reach between 40 and 50 millions. Judging by the way in which the minister has slammed the door on immigration these days I do not think our population will be anywhere near 40 or 50 million people by that date.
We were assured that access roads to the north would be built and that the government would provide $15 million to the provinces towards this end. A railroad was to be built into the north; a road program for the Yukon and the Northwest Territories was going to cost $100 million and, in addition, a federal-provincial cost-sharing program of access roads would, in the words of one minister, cost $75 million-in fact, he got so excited he said it might even be $150 million.

The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) predicted that the program of road building in northern Canada would mean employment for hundreds of thousands of Canadians. The retired employees of Canadian railroads were assured that their demands for pension increases would receive full consideration. We were assured that one of the first acts in the session of the twenty-fourth parliament would be to abolish the rule of closure in Commons debates. We in the province of British Columbia were assured that there would be a joint investment program or other sound financial assistance in the development of Columbia river power. Nothing has been heard of that. Of course, we could not expect anything very definite in March because we were told that no basis of finality could be arrived at until the month of October. October has come and gone and we still have not heard of any basis of finality.
The co-operative movement was assured that the Conservative party would encourage it in every way. Mr. Speaker, I know that movement so well that I can safely say that this government has done absolutely nothing in regard to this particular election promise. We were assured that the leader of the government had very much in mind a second trans-Canada highway. At a later meeting he became a little more excited and added the words "at the earliest possible date". However, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) told us in effect during the last session that we would not be getting any second trans-Canada highway until we had finished the first one and, as he well knows, one of the provinces of Canada has not even begun the first one yet, so the rest of Canada is going to be held up once more in the development of a necessary project because other parts of Canada are slow.
The textile workers were assured that no industry would be subject to the ill effects of dumping. Fruit and vegetable growers were assured that they, too, would be protected against dumping and against the importation of earlier ripening vegetables and fruit. We were told the Canada Elections Act would be amended to reduce the time allowed for election campaigns; we were told that advance poll provisions would be widened so that more than three classifications of citizens could take advantage of the advance poll; we were assured that Canada would assert her sovereignty over her northern territories. Absolutely nothing has been done. A lot of violent anti-American feeling has been aroused, it is true, but no single action has been taken to assure Canadian sovereignty


over her northern territories. Indeed, if anything has been done, the signing of the NORAD agreement has robbed us of some of our sovereignty over our northern territories.
We were assured that by processing in Canada to the largest degree possible all our raw materials we would no longer have to ship them to the United States. I have yet to hear any minister rise in his place and mention one single thing which this government has done to prevent the continuing and growing export from Canada of our raw material resources. Our provincial governments were assured of a new deal and, for a time, we were almost fooled. Sixty-two million dollars more was given to the provincial governments. However, because of the decline in revenue, $50 million of the $62 million has already been lost to the provinces, and the recent rise in interest rates has caused the provincial governments to lose even more. So that under the present government the provinces will get less than they received hitherto under the Liberal government. The municipalities, of course, did not get a new deal at all as they had been led to believe. On October 6 and 7 they were told to go home and raise their tax rates and assessments; they were told that if they could not sell their bonds and debentures they ought to consider carefully raising the interest rates offered.
Our fishermen were assured that they would receive the benefit of floor prices fixed with regard to the cost of production. Nothing has been done about that. A firm stand was promised with regard to the protection of Canadian inshore fisheries against foreign trawlers. Again, nothing has been done about that; the Icelandic government is the only government which has taken a firm stand. We have yet to see what action this government will take to remove discrimination in the matter of freight rates. We were assured that the tight money policy of the former government would be reversed. In fact, exactly the opposite has taken place.
We were assured that interest rates were needlessly high. They are even higher today. In fact, this government handed on a silver platter to the moneylenders of Canada an undeserved gift which over the course of the next twenty-five years, using the Minister of Finance's own figures, will amount to over $1,000 million. That is how the government handles the taxpayers' money with respect to moneylenders but when it comes to the unemployed the government says, "we have to fight inflation and balance the budget."
The Conservatives assured us they would call a conference on national conservation in

the fall of 1958 but that has not been done. They assured us that the application of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act would be extended to all parts of Canada but that has not been done. They told us in certain terms something would be done about the natural gas pipeline but nothing has been done except the appointment of a royal commission. They held out to the people of Newfoundland the hope of aid for the development of hydro power projects and the building of transmission lines. We know what has been done in this respect.
In the city of Vancouver last March we were assured that as far as the recession was concerned we had passed the peak. I find it difficult to believe that the Prime Minister of Canada, a responsible and highly respected man, could look at the figures and statistics and read the economic and business barometers and shout out to an audience of 13,000 that they are to ignore all these facts because, "I, the Prime Minister, personally assure you we are past the peak." Mr. Speaker, the mills of God grind slowly but they grind exceeding fine.
I remember one other prime minister who in an election in the 1930 campaign put bands of honor on the arms of the unemployed but the revenge came in 1935 and that man went out with a bigger bang than that with which he came in. This may well happen on the Canadian scene five years following the last election.
We were assured that the province of Quebec could rest content in the knowledge that its provincial rights would be safeguarded and cabinet representation from that province would be respected. I notice no leading member of the present cabinet representing that one-third of the Canadian population in the province of Quebec. We were also assured that Canada would not allow United States domination of Canadian industrial enterprise. Absolutely nothing has been done in this regard.
How the Conservatives wept for the plight of the small businessman but there is no indication that financial aid will be made available so that he can expand his business. He was assured of credit so he could expand and meet his larger competitors on more equitable terms. Nothing has been done. The sum of $30,000 was voted in the estimates last year which is enough to build one filling station in one small village in Canada. That illustrates the sympathy this government has shown toward small business.
One of the most pathetic cases of all is that affecting the old age pensioners of Canada and the understanding they had of what might be done for them by this government.
The Address-Mr. Regier I attended some of their meetings just before the new year. Many pensioners mentioned the fact that this government is going to bring in a new social security system and they are hopeful that the Prime Minister will keep that election promise and that they will receive a higher income. What a terrible hoax this is because the implementation of the Clark report or any other report setting up a new national insurance plan will result in the government saying to these old people now on pension, "Look, folks, you did not pay anything into it. This has to be on an actuarial basis so just be content to continue receiving what you now get." It is an appalling thing to mislead these old age pensioners into thinking their cash income will be increased if the government has no intention of doing so.
We were assured that taxation would be revised downward. First of all there would be a radical income tax change affecting most Canadians. There was the vague promise of a tobacco tax cut. Our investors were to be placed on an equal footing with foreigners. We were assured that this government would recapture foreign markets that had been lost, would begin trade with the Chinese communists and would take some trading eggs out of the United States basket. I do not think any minister can cite a single action of this government that has been taken to implement those election promises in regard to recovering our foreign markets.
And then we had the election promise of them all. We all remember how that five-cent piece used to haunt Mackenzie King. I think he had a nickel in his pocket when he was buried. How we heard about that in the 1930 election campaign. But there is another election promise that is going to haunt some people in Canada and it is to the effect that no man or woman is going to suffer from unemployment. I give fair warning that as long as there are unemployed in this country there will be C.C.F. members in this house to rub it in time and time again until this government realizes that it cannot ride out the storm, that the situation is extremely serious and the government is responsible for the welfare of the Canadian people. Certainly an unemployed man sleeping under newspapers in a public place cannot be told he is not going to suffer from unemployment.
I have omitted the pledges made by members of this government to those interested in education or with respect to the rights of parliament, Senate reform or the question of removing the review of divorce from the House of Commons but I feel I have listed enough clear illustrations to demonstrate the record of the government in terms of keeping its election promises.

I say the government cannot deliver the goods because it is enslaved to the moneylenders of Canada. That is so obvious. Its one major economic influence since it took office has been the bond conversion deal. It found $30,000 for the small businessman; $9 million for education and although I do not know what its winter works program will cost I know from personal observation it will not be too much. This government was able to find $1,000 million for the moneylenders of this country and as a result the interest rate will be raised for every provincial and municipal government, hospital and school board, every business enterprise and every individual in Canada.
