The history of the monetary system in Canada in years to come will bear out what I have now said.
The old philosophy that he governs best who governs least is completely obsolete today. Those who subscribe to that philosophy should move into the heart of Africa where there is no government or taxes. Adequate government and a growing concept of the role of government are marks of civilization. The people of Canada will some day realize they will get nothing from the Conservative government and this will be true because they did not sacrifice to elect the present government. Rather the advertising agencies and moneylenders of Canada elected this government and as long as people are willing to sit back and allow vested interests to elect their parliament so long will the people derive little benefit from parliament. They will get only as much as those in office feel they must give in order to once more lure their vote away from them at election time.

Mr. Speaker, may I first express the sense of privilege which I feel in returning to this House of Commons as the member for York Centre and in having the opportunity of taking part in the work of parliament.

I would first congratulate my friend, the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee), on the fighting speech he made at the commencement of to-day's proceedings, in which he set out so clearly the measures taken by this administration in the past 18 months to meet the problems of the nation.
I would also like to express my congratulations to the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia (Mr. McPhillips), who gave us just a little while ago such a colourful account of the history of his province and of the problems affecting his native city of Victoria. I am sure that many hon. members long after they have left this house and in their old age will remember that speech and read it in Hansard, as I will, with a great deal of pleasure.
These are exciting and critical days and the things that we decide here will have important effects not only on the people of this country but on many people throughout the world. For this reason, I consider it a privilege to be here.
In recent months I have met and talked to a number of people who have come to this country from Europe and other places. They are grateful for the material advantages they find in this country but the most precious thing to them is the freedom which they have in Canada. This parliament is the guardian not only of many of the rights that make up this freedom but it is also the symbol of our democratic tradition. For this reason also I consider it a privilege to be here.
The citizens of Canada, Mr. Speaker, are expecting great things of us in this second session of the twenty-fourth parliament. The problems facing us are complex and in many ways unique. The working out of solutions will require industry, insight and, if I may say so, a certain measure of restraint in the matter of speech-making. We are here primarily to get things done. And, Mr. Speaker, no hysterical, emotional speeches such as we have just listened to from the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) will assist us at all in the solution of those problems. I listened to that speech with careful attention and I must say that in the whole of it there was not one positive, creative idea presented which would assist the administration in the solution of the great problems facing this country.

May I also express my respect for the colleagues of the Prime Minister who share with him the responsibility of government. I think I have some little idea of the weight of the obligations they have and the constant pressures which surround them. I have said on the hustings and I say here that these are ministers of whom every Canadian can be proud.
I think that the Canadian people expect us to do two principal things during this session: first, to take measures which will promote prosperity and, secondly, to adopt policies and to take actions which will help promote peace in the world. Notwithstanding a slow beginning, 1958 turned out to be a better year than many observers predicted. Our gross national product increased by two per cent. Total exports remained almost unchanged from the year before. Wheat exports increased by almost 50 million bushels. Farm implement sales were greater than the year before. There was also a substantial decrease in our world trade deficit. Personal incomes of Canadians-and this term includes many thousands of Canadians represented by our friends to Your Honour's left-rose by about five per cent and consumer spending was four per cent higher than the year before.
While these are substantial achievements, Mr. Speaker, there are still thousands of Canadian out of work, and it is the first responsibility of this parliament to assist business and industry in the solution of the problem of unemployment. I sometimes think that "problem" in this connection is a pretty inadequate word; for it fails so badly to describe the distress and misery that a man goes through when he cannot find a job.
Equally disturbing is the problem of inflation, which is recognized as the basic danger to the health of our economy by every re-ponsible leader in business and in the trade union movement. One of the contributing factors, of course, has been the increase in the money supply, a 12 per cent increase in the one-year period beginning October 1, 1957. While this increase had some effect in speeding the economic recovery, it is a trend that
The Address-Mr. Stinson must be stopped. Another factor has been the huge spending program on the part of governments at all levels. I think we have to learn that the transfer of money from one sector of the tax-paying public to another does not necessarily produce wealth and that it can have serious inflationary effects.
The only effective answer to inflation is increased production and increased production is achieved only when people work harder and improve their techniques. No democratic country can undertake to force people to do these things. It is our responsibility as individual Canadians to accept higher incomes only when we have earned those incomes by greater productive effort.
One of the major reasons for the economic upturn in many parts of the country has been the government's policy with respect to housing. In the first half of 1957 there was a serious decline in residential construction. Upon coming to power this government introduced legislation which had the effect of requiring a lower down payment and lower income eligibility of people applying for loans under the National Housing Act. More than half a billion dollars has been made available for the construction of houses and other residential units. The government has encouraged limited dividend projects providing low rental housing and the redevelopment of depressed areas in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities.
These policies, Mr. Speaker, have resulted in a spectacular record for residential construction, with housing starts in the year 1958 reaching 163,000, one-third more than the figure for 1957. In my own community of North York township the value of buildings for which permits were issued last year rose to $130 million as against $76 million in 1957, with 10,000 new dwelling units being commenced during the year. It is impossible, of course, to estimate the social effects of this policy of promoting home ownership. The economic effects are felt throughout the whole economy. Serious problems remain. The high cost of serviced land in the suburban areas makes it difficult to build houses at prices that can be paid by low income workers. While municipalities have the major responsibility in this field, this government and the members of this party recognize the need for assistance.
Perhaps the most significant step taken by the government in recent months was the convening of the commonwealth trade and economic conference in Montreal. Here was a meeting of the representatives of 600 million people living in that unique family of nations known as the British commonwealth. Much was achieved. It was agreed
112	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Stinson that it was desirable to expand the resources of the international bank and the international monetary fund. It now appears that there will be a substantial increase in the resources of each of these important international financial agencies. The government of the United Kingdom announced the removal of dollar import restrictions from raw materials and industrial machinery. It was agreed that consideration should be given to the problem of the disposal of subsidized surplus products so that the legitimate markets of the members of the commonwealth would not be impaired. One of the major accomplishments, of course, was the recognition by all representatives of the need for more rapid economic development of the underdeveloped countries. I think we can all take great satisfaction in the increase in Colombo plan aid recently announced by the Prime Minister of this country.
This record certainly is good but, Mr. Speaker, it is still a fact that in this country and in all the western countries we have not yet begun to realize what is going on in the other half of the world in science, in industrial production and in education. While we in this country have been concentrating on becoming more comfortable, reducing our hours of work and finding amusements for our leisure time, the Russians and the Chinese are changing the face of the world. Not only that, but the Russians have reached out into the heavens and a man-made planet is now making its way around the sun. Consider, for example, the comparative figures for the production of steel. In 1958, Great Britain produced 18,902,000 tons of steel, 3 million tons less than was produced the year before. Canada produced 4,359,000 tons, about 2 million tons less than her capacity. The United States produced 85 million tons as compared with 112,700,000 tons the year before. Russia in 1958 produced 60 million tons, an increase of 4.5 million tons over 1957. Production in China was
10,700,000	tons, an increase over 1957 production of 4,800,000 tons.
These are plain facts, which are not changed by conversation about low wage rates and the long working hours of the Russian and Chinese workers. The spectacular achievements of Russia in the scientific fields are well known. Less well known are the accomplishments of the Chinese. Professor J. T. Wilson, who was in China last summer, has recently reported in the Saturday Review on a visit he made to the city of Lanchow. Here, in a city of 800,000 people, there has been established a scientific centre where within 10 years 15,000 technical people will be employed. He saw a library containing


2,600 science periodicals. The equipment was of a high quality and much of the work under the direction of western-trained scientists.
If we fail in this race against the Russians and the Chinese and the other Asian countries we will fail because we have become lazy, fat and complacent. Nowhere have we become more complacent than in the field of education. Last summer I had the opportunity of reading a report made by a young Canadian teacher, Mr. Anthony Frisch, who has made a careful study of the curriculum of the East German and soviet high schools in science and mathematics. Mr. Frisch has studied at Cambridge and McGill universities and has been a classroom teacher in Ontario schools. His report compares the soviet and East German curriculum with that in each of the provinces of Canada.
He points out that in Ontario the courses in mathematics are behind the soviet courses by about three years in the soviet equivalent of grades 9 and 10. In physics, Ontario is behind the soviet by two years in the soviet equivalent of grade 7; one year in the soviet equivalent of grade 9; one year in the soviet equivalent of grade 10; and one to two years in the first part of the soviet equivalent of grade 11. In Ontario, there is no attempt to teach mathematical molecular physics and the thermodynamics which are taught in the Russian counterpart of grade 11. In chemistry, Mr. Frisch reports Russian children are taught more in two years than Ontario children in five. In the final year in Russia, the whole course is devoted to organic chemistry, whereas in Ontario the upper school course includes only three weeks' work in this subject.
In British Columbia, Mr. Frisch reports that in mathematics the courses trail the soviet courses by three years and that the matters covered in the final two years of the soviet high schools are not touched at all. In physics, most of the work taught in the final 2J years of the soviet high schools is not attempted at all.
In the Atlantic provinces, the teaching of mathematics and science falls even further behind what is being done in the Russian high schools. In Russia there are 71 subject units taught in mathematics, physics, chemistry and biology in the secondary schools, and in the provinces of Canada the figures are as follows:
British Columbia	 34
Alberta	   42
Saskatchewan	 43
Manitoba	 40
Ontario	 54
Quebec (Protestant	schools)	 48
Quebec (Catholic schools)	 28
Atlantic provinces		 42
Newfoundland	 27

This concentration on intensive training in science and mathematics is not confined to countries under the Russian influence. In the Gymnasia Ivrit secondary school in Jerusalem, the curriculum taught in these subjects is similar to that given in the schools in Russia and in East Germany, and this in a country struggling to meet the basic material needs of the people.
It is my opinion that three things are urgently needed. The first is a vigorous effort on the part of ministers of education to revise the curriculum in mathematics and science. I am persuaded that such a step would be well received by the secondary school students of this country, many of whom would prefer a more exacting curriculum to some of the extra-curricular amusements which are offered up these days.
Second, we require more public money to be spent on education, for equipment, for teachers and for scholarships. At the present time ten per cent of the money spent each year for national defence would pay the total budget for education in the province of Ontario.
Finally, we need to arouse the people of the country to an awareness that this matter has become a national crisis.
As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said last summer at the Couchiching conference, "crisis" is a very common noun these days, partly because it fits neatly into a headline. As we read the newspapers, every day seems to bring a new crisis. I suggest, however, that some of the most critical things which are happening seldom reach the headlines, and that this falling behind in education is one of them.
I would also propose that in addition to the scholarships agreed upon at the commonwealth trade and economic conference, this government establish awards for study in other parts of the commonwealth in science and in history, the recipients to be known as "commonwealth scholars". While there may be constitutional difficulties in the way of federal government action in this field of education, I think these can be overcome if the Canadian people can be brought to realize that their children and grandchildren may not be equipped to meet conditions in the world as they will find them.
Mr. Speaker, I have touched on some of the things which I believe to require attention in this session. In a free country governments alone do not determine whether or not our goals are achieved. Much depends on the will, the enterprise and the judgment of individual citizens. Government policies and actions, however, remain terribly important. It is our duty as private members in all
The Address-Mr. Godin parties to recommend to the government of the day policies and actions which we think advisable.
We are living in an important era in the history of our country, and we cannot permit ourselves to become downhearted or easily discouraged. I was reading the other day, on the wall of the office of a good friend of mine, a few lines written by Edmund Burke which were as follows:
Those who would carry on great public schemes must be proof against the most fatiguing delays, the most mortifying disappointments, the most shocking insults and, worst of all, the presumptuous judgment of the ignorant upon their designs.
While I believe this statement to be true, I also believe that all of us in this House of Commons can receive great rewards, rewards that will come from great public schemes courageously undertaken.

Mr. Speaker, I am most pleased that I am being given such an early opportunity to speak in the debate on the speech from the throne so that I may give to members of this house an on-the-spot account concerning the great economic difficulties which our area necessarily suffered since the last session of this parliament.
At the outset I must say that I fully realize that the problem was a provincial one and that, primarily, it had to be settled at the conference table by the union and the management. However, I am pleased to pay tribute in this house to the union of mine, mill and smelter workers, local 598, for the manner in which the strike was undertaken and carried out. As far as I have been able to read in the newspapers, we in our area all feel confident that the strike was carried out with the best of discipline. I am also pleased to congratulate the company which at that time was necessarily faced with a problem. We heard yesterday that there was no existing problem of recession or inflation. I feel that the workers in my area in the face of the rising cost of living, were definitely entitled to make demands for higher wages, something which they have been accustomed to do. I also fully realize that the company, in the face of the present recession and in view of the figures on its books, could not very well afford to increase the cost of its production. That is why I am pleased to offer to both the congratulations which they deserve. Later in my address I will speak of the problem involved, but first I should like to state how greatly the population of our area have appreciated the assistance from the Catholic charities, the Salvation Army and the newspaper Le Droit

The Address-Mr. Godin of Ottawa. All have made charitable donations for the purpose of assisting the needy people in crises of this nature.
Yesterday we had the privilege of hearing three extremely important speeches. As a newcomer in this twenty-fourth parliament, I must say how greatly I was impressed by the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the manner in which he described to this parliament the problems of today. It is my intention to say a few words later about the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) but, if I may be permitted to do so, I should like to discuss the less important matters first.
I should like to make a few remarks about the position of the C.C.F. group in the house. At the beginning of his speech the leader of the C.C.F. group said that as far as he was concerned there was no difference in the speeches delivered by the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister and that if they were to change seats in the house all they would have to do would be to exchange notes. I understand this is possible because it is a known fact that the Canadian people have never required the C.C.F. group either to undertake the duties of government or of the official opposition.
The role of the C.C.F. group may be similar to that of an old maid who would undertake to give advice to a young bride on the intricacies and difficulties of marriage. I have heard the further reference that possibly the C.C.F. group in this house may be compared with a drum majorette. There is much high kicking and twirling but the sound does not come from there. The music of proper policies for our country is very confused unless the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) would like to have the house believe that the advantages or disadvantages of queen bee jelly are a major Canadian problem.
Before I go further I should like to take the opportunity to congratulate the young member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) for the wonderful contribution he made in moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I trust that the hon. member may have further opportunities to present to the house the opinions which he elaborated so well.

Possibly his speech was slightly different from last year in the sense that he took ten minutes to introduce remarks concerning his trip around the world, but my recollection is that the only reference made to that tour since the house began was in the form of congratulations by two members who said we were happy to see him return in good health after such a strenuous and possibly fruitful visit. The Address-Mr. Godin
Now in referring to this heritage which this present government claims it has received, I wish briefly to describe conditions around Nickel Belt. Firstly, however, may I say we fully recall a certain heritage in the history of Canada, and that was the one left in 1935. We all know that the talk of those days was not gloom and doom; the talk of those days was to rebuild Canada and to bring about the solution of social problems for which I am sure hon. members of the C.C.F. party were very happy to vote- such measures as family allowances and unemployment insurance. This was done, and the Liberal government carried Canada through an awful heritage, through the prewar period, through a very difficult war which was the costliest Canada has ever known, and through an equally difficult postwar period. This, the Canadian people all remember. The Prime Minister has produced statistics to show that everything is on the upswing, that there is no recession and no inflation. I have statistics of my own; they may not be all figures, but they are facts, and I think facts sometimes speak much better than figures.
The people in my area refer to the policy of the present government as an accordion policy; you squeeze both ends against the middle, and in the middle are the Canadian people. I say this because the facts I shall give will bear it out. We had a wealthy industry in our area in the Nickel Belt but the recession is doing something to it. The workers were accustomed to making demands for increases, and they did make those demands on account of inflation and the rising cost of living, but they could not obtain satisfaction. I must say this, and it is a known fact in my area: since the Conservative party came into power 11 voting subdivisions have been closed because lumbering industries have been closed and because there are no people living there. In addition, mines have closed and, with regret, I must say that four mines have been closed in my own area since the Conservative party came to power. These may not be statistics but they are facts. I say with regret that the Conservative candidate who opposed me was an employee of one of those mines which have closed, and that he became unemployed thereby.
The Prime Minister indicated to this house that he did not follow the calculation of the Leader of the Opposition when he stated that the old age pensioners had lost $2 of their pensions. I think I can better this, Mr. Speaker. Visiting my riding a short while ago I met an old gentleman of about 72. He had three sons. Of course, we discussed politics as people usually do when they meet their representative in parliament, and he stated

The Address-Mr. Godin that he was a supporter of the present government and that he was impressed by the $9-that was the major reason for his support of the party. That was his confession to me. He told me he wanted me to meet his three sons. I was introduced to the three sons, all fathers of young families, and then he said: "Sir, these three boys had been working steadily for 15 years, earning $300 a month each. What happened was I got my $9 by voting for the present government, but my family has lost $900 a month." That speaks more strongly than statistics.
Now I turn to the Inco strike. As I said earlier, I fully realize that this is a provincial matter and that it involves a dispute between labour and management, but the cause is very interesting to seek. What actually happened? Hon. members can check Hansard for last year, and they will find that when I had occasion to make my first speech in this house I asked the government to give us the accustomed Liberal prosperity, in which case they would solve 85 per cent of the problems in my riding. We have known for many years that we are a wealthy section, but we also know that we could lose all that very quickly. The people of my area remember what happened last fall. How did it occur?
The workers were asking for more because the cost of living was higher, and that was correct. However, the company felt that it could not increase its cost of production at that time because they had lost markets, possibly due to the diversion scheme, and because they were not able to sell to the extent they were selling before. Here I have a copy of a brief in which is set out a good foundation for the understanding of the problem which arose in the nickel industry. After 18 pages of statistics and an analysis of the conditions facing the company, the submission concludes with a passage which I would be pleased to call as a witness and make part of Hansard. It is the conclusion of the brief presented to the conciliation board, and I quote:
These current conditions have been clearly reflected in the company's profits. As compared with 1956, the year in which the last negotiations with the unions took place-
That is true. The last negotiations in the area in the industry took place in 1956 before this government was elected.
-the net earnings for 1957 were down by an amount in excess of $10 million. So far as the first quarter of 1958 is concerned, the net earnings were little more than one-half the net earnings for the same quarter in 1957. The net earnings for the second quarter of 1958 are substantially less than one-half the net earnings for the second quarter of 1957. In short, the net earnings of this

company for the first six months of 1958 are $21,401,000 as compared with $45,601,000 for the first six months of 1957-
And listen to this:
-and compared with $51,772,000 for the first six months of 1956.
That is the heritage which was left in 1956, and that is what the present government has done to it. I may say, further, that in a notice published in the local newspaper the company repeated the difficulties which it was encountering, and we read the following paragraph:
Against this background it was obvious that the company could not raise its production costs by continuing the unbroken record of substantial increases in wages and fringe benefits it had maintained over the past 14 years.
That is the heritage about which we are now complaining. That is what happened. Crude statistics cannot compare with a proper review of conditions in the Nickel Belt area.
On many occasions I have had the pleasure of discussing with municipal officials the problems with which they are confronted. It has been announced that within a few weeks that a program of winter work will come into effect to cure various problems. What problems will this cure? Winter work is nothing but relief. We are all happy to accept winter work for our municipalities because there is no doubt that the unemployed must find a means of providing food for their families but the tendency to rely on this type of program as a remedy for situations of this kind is an old routine. In my younger days I was employed in the same fashion under the Bennett regime digging ditches on highways and cutting brush along creeks. A program of this kind is not a valid solution to the problem which the Canadian people expect this government to solve.
The people of this country do not wish to be kennel dogs living off unemployment relief or family allowance checks and give-away winter jobs lasting three weeks. The Canadian worker wants instead to be a bird dog, one that can go out and catch a bird and thus feather the nest for his family. They want the opportunity of securing permanent employment. I realize that the unemployed worker must accept the employment offered him under programs of this kind in order to provide for the immediate needs of his family but his ambition is to find permanent work. I am surprised that the attitude of the present government should be one of patting the unemployed worker on the head and telling him not to worry because the winter works program will soon come into effect. The government has had many opportunities in the last seventeen months to undertake constructive measures to meet this situation. The attitudes

The Address-Mr. Weichel
presently displayed by members of the government are those we have witnessed before and they do nothing to alleviate the hardships created by the problem of unemployment.
A matter of some interest to the people of my riding is the objection this government had to a motion which I had occasion to bring forth at the time when the question of income tax deductions was under discussion in this house. A little bait was introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in that the cost of an ambulance to a licensed hospital was to become deductible from income tax. I have discussed this with people in my riding and they asked me to come back and tell this government to amend this statute further. The deductibility of fees for ambulances to licensed hospitals extends to a small group in Canada and applies to a group that does not need such assistance. We know that ambulance service exists only in the larger centres in Canada and extends only within five or ten miles of a licensed hospital.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of the older of the new members, I wish to congratulate you, your deputy and the chairman on your appointments to the important positions you hold in this house. In your office as Speaker you have the responsibility of upholding the rights of both the minority and the majority and we are all confident that you will as you have demonstrated in the past.
This is my maiden speech, Mr. Speaker, and I deem it a great honour to be standing up here in the House of Commons only a few seats from where my uncle, the late W. G. Weichel, sat more than two score years ago. As a young boy, I avidly followed the career of my uncle in parliament and never dreamed that some day I would succeed him. As it turned out, I was elected the first Conservative member in my constituency since my uncle was defeated in 1917. I hope that my stay here in Ottawa will be as productive as was that of my uncle and that he, as the parliamentarian he was, will be proud of my efforts here. Even over that long span of 41 years, there are still members in this house, like the hon. member from Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) who remember my uncle in parliament.
I would like to add my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the speech from the throne. I am sure that the country will hail the many worthwhile things the government expects to do in this session as outlined in the throne speech. Probably of most significance to my riding of Waterloo North were the planned aid to farmers, the boost for home building and the assistance to exporters, veterans and the unemployed.
The many exporters in my industrial riding of Waterloo North probably see much good

The Address-Mr. Weichel in the government's aim to change the Export Credits Insurance Act, which will help to insure them against non-payment by foreign buyers. Farmers, too, gained much hope from the contents of the throne speech. The move to institute farm crop insurance and the planned review and revision of farm credit legislation should be a boon to my agriculture-conscious riding, as well as to others.
Although Waterloo North has not been hard hit by unemployment, the changes proposed in the Unemployment Insurance Act prove the intention of this government to deal effectively with this problem. I cannot pass by this opportunity to congratulate the government on its proposal to establish a national energy board. Oil and natural gas interests have been awaiting this move and the formation of such a body will regulate the proper use of these important resources.
Before giving hon. members an outline of the highlights of my constituency I would like to say that it has produced some of Canada's greatest statesmen. The long-time prime minister Mackenzie King was born in Kitchener. His birthplace "Woodside" has been maintained by citizens who honoured and respected him. The hon. member of the Senate, W. D. Euler, was elected to this house in 1917, and since that time has sat either here or in the Senate. To continue my relationship with former members in this house, the Hon. Mr. Euler is my cousin. Not a relative, but a close friend and distinguished statesman, the Hon. Louis O. Breithaupt is also Waterloo North born and bred. As hon. members know, he served Waterloo North for many years before being elevated to the post of lieutenant governor of the province of Ontario. Another friend was my predecessor, Norman C. Schneider, who is known to many hon. members here. An old army buddy of mine in the first world war, Mr. Schneider served the constituency well during his stay here.
Waterloo North, which I inherited from Mr. Schneider, is one of the most heavily concentrated areas in Ontario in both industry and population. It boasts one of the best farming areas in the dominion. Waterloo North was settled by Mennonites of Pennsylvania German extraction, who came to our district on a 600-mile-long trek in Conestoga wagons from Pennsylvania. They were joined by British settlers and down through the years by Polish, Ukrainian, Hungarian, German, Austrian, Italian, Jewish and many others, making this one of the most cosmopolitan centres in Canada. The Mennonites of the district, a sect not unlike the Quakers, have stayed on and today operate a big portion of the rich farms of Waterloo North.

The twin communities of Kitchener and Waterloo, with a total population of some
80,000,	are the largest municipalities in my constituency. These two cities have a total of 280 firms manufacturing hundreds of diversified products. Kitchener, the larger centre, has 205 industries, with a yearly production valued at $181,321,000, a figure which places this city fourth in Ontario and ninth in the Dominion of Canada. Gross value of production has increased over 100 per cent since 1944.
With a large acreage of land now available for industrial expansion, indications are that many more firms from the United States, England and continental Europe will settle in the city. Many of those which now rate as the city's leading industries had humble beginnings and are managed at the present time by third or fourth generation descendants of the original founders.
Probably Kitchener's best-known industries are its rubber and meat packing firms. The meat packing plants are J. M. Schneider Limited and Burns and Company (Eastern) Limited. The rubber industries, B. F. Goodrich Canada Limited, Dominion Rubber Company of Canada and Kaufman Rubber Company, along with Kitchener Button Industries Limited, hailed the government's move last year to tighten anti-dumping laws. It was proof to them that the Conservative government is interested in all their problems. However, leaders of these firms and others look for more assistance in the future.
Another young and thriving industry in this city is the Dominion Electrohome Industries Limited which has expanded considerably recently because of the publics interest in its products, namely television and electronic devices.
In an effort to keep these factories humming, the Kitchener chamber of commerce has designated February 13 to February 23 as Kitchener's products week. Every retail store in the city will donate a window for the display of products made by Kitchener workmen. To lend novelty to the mass merchandising display, a jewellery store will display meat products, for example, and possibly a ladies' wear store will show tires. It is hoped that the displays will encourage area consumers to buy Kitchener-made goods and keep the home town workmen busy throughout what is usually the peak unemployment season.
Kitchener's twin sister, Waterloo, is probably best known as the Hartford of Canada. Within its borders are the head offices of six insurance companies employing about 1,500 people. Total assets of these companies exceed $750 million. No other city in Canada has

such a large percentage of its economic activity embodied in the insurance business. Their business covers the length and breadth of Canada and includes branches in several foreign countries.
Although insurance rates as Waterloo's chief industry, the city's fame has also been spread through the manufacture of alcoholic beverages. Joseph E. Seagram and Sons Limited, which celebrated its hundredth anniversary last year, has grown to become the world's largest distiller. The Seagram organization includes not only six large plants in Canada but others in the United States, Scotland, Jamaica and Puerto Rico.
On the other side of the thirst-quenching scale, Waterloo also produces beer from the large concern of Carling Breweries Limited. It employs 385 people in its Waterloo plant and its annual payroll is $1,450,000. Another well-known brewery, Dow-Kingsbeer, makes its home in Kitchener.
Waterloo College associate faculties is the centre of one of the newest experiments in higher education being conducted in Canada. Two years ago it introduced a co-operative engineering course that combines periods in the classroom with alternate stays in industry. The co-operative plan, revolutionary in Canadian education, has focussed a great deal of interest on the Waterloo College campus. By 1965 the college which now has close to 1,000 students expects to expand to have an enrolment of 3,500. Coupled with this is an energetic construction program which will give the campus 19 new buildings in the next seven years. It is expected early in the new year that the Waterloo institution will be given a degree-granting charter and become Waterloo university.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

May I continue my remarks about the city of Waterloo, Mr. Speaker? Waterloo is also the home of the biggest band festival in Canada, and probably in the world. This band festival yearly attracts to the city between 15,000 and 20,000 people and provides competition for over 1,000 young musicians taking part in the brass, bugle, trumpet and reed bands as well as individual competitions, a real worthwhile effort to assist our youth in music. This year some 80 bands from Canada and the United States took part in the three-hour long parade to Seagram stadium, a $250,000 structure donated to the city last year on the occasion of the Seagram firm's centennial.
The Address-Mr. Weichel
While there naturally is friendly rivalry between cities set so close together, there is also co-operation. The cities derive the benefit of a common hospital, a common secondary school educational system, trolley bus service, orphanage, service clubs and sports organizations. Thousands of Kitchener and Waterloo residents travel between the two cities daily to and from their employment. As an illustration of the complexity of the situation, I may say that only a few years ago the mayor of Waterloo worked in Kitchener, while the mayor of Kitchener lived in Waterloo. Twin city residents are proud of their homes and they are great churchgoers. More than 90 per cent of the people belong to the many churches situated there, and the cities rank among the top three in Canada in home ownership.
In discussing my constituency, I cannot forget my home town of Elmira where I was supervisory postmaster for over 35 years. I might say that at the moment my brother is the mayor of Elmira. It is a thriving little centre of some 3,000 people and its largest industry is the Naugatuck Chemical Company which pioneered in the production, so far as the British empire is concerned, of a type of synthetic rubber, 2-4D, and D.D.T. Under the direction of the Elmira recreational council, this town has won some 15 Ontario hockey association and Ontario minor hockey association championships. The Ontario minor hockey association, of which I had the privilege of being president in 1952 and 1954, is the largest minor hockey organization in the world, and sponsors almost 30,000 boys yearly. I might mention too that it has been my privilege to be associated with the Ontario hockey association, and the Toronto hockey league, two of the finest organizations in the world.
Whatever I am now, and whatever I have been in life, Mr. Speaker, there are two things I most assuredly am, a sportsman and a veteran. There is a tie-up between those two things because it was the loss of my right leg in the trenches during the first world war that cut short a possible professional sports career for me. It is on these two subjects, sports and the world of veterans, that I should like to speak now.
In the last few years international sports have become of increasing importance to countries. Russia, which has made amazing strides militarily, economically and scientifically in the past three decades, has vaulted into the spotlight of the sports world through its Olympic victories. Canada, too, has gained a good share of that spotlight, largely through the winnings and losings of her hockey teams

The Address-Mr. Weichel in international competition. My own constituency of Waterloo North was proud to send its Kitchener-Waterloo Dutchmen to Cortina in 1956 to compete in the Olympic games. Although the Dutchmen lost, they added to Canada's stature by the good impressions they made in Europe when they played in Germany, Czechoslovakia, France, Holland, Italy and Great Britain. Everywhere they went they were hailed as sportsmen, fine competitors and good ambassadors for this country. Mr. George Dudley, veteran secretary-manager of the Canadian amateur hockey association announced on January 2 that the Kitchener-Waterloo Dutchmen were named as Canadian representatives to compete in the 1960 winter games at Squaw Valley, California. They will be noteworthy representatives of Canada, Mr. Speaker.
These teams are always hampered by lack of funds. While the governments of other countries back sports development programs financially, our federal governments so far have offered no encouragement to athletics. The big stumbling block is money. It takes a lot to provide adequate facilities and operate a development plan. So far the federal governments have not assumed any portion of the costs of either training athletes or sending them to international competitions. Organizations such as the Canadian amateur hockey association in hockey and the Canadian Legion in track and field, and individuals, have had to carry the heavy financial burden. It is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that it is now time for our government to take a look at things. A ministry of sports and athletic development might be the answer. With government assistance, we might reach the day when we could send national teams abroad without forcing their leaders to go begging for funds to make the trip.
Millions of dollars are spent each year on cultural development in this country. I am in total accord with this, as any fair-minded sportsman would be. I also feel, however, we should spend a similar amount on the physical and athletic development of our young Canadians. Let the government look at the by-product of sports events. There is the goodwill the competition fosters for Canada; the easing of international tension through international sports; the raising of the prestige of the country through participation; and the example the sportsmen on these teams set for our youth. So far Canada has not achieved the place in international competition which the potential we have warrants. However, with proper assistance that goal is attainable.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, I am a veteran, and as a veteran I have strong feelings about Remembrance Day and its observance. Although I feel in my own heart that a day with such resounding significance as November 11 should be observed as a holiday,
I realize that this is not the wish of all veterans' organizations. Both these organizations, however-and I join them-strongly urge the government to lead the country in a proper observance of this day that means so much to us. Perhaps the main thing this government can do is to stifle any move to shift the observance of November 11 to the nearest Sunday. If the observance of this occasion were moved to any other day, it would be to brush off with little thought the contribution our veterans have made by laying down their lives for our freedom. I, as a veteran who has hobbled on one leg for longer than I walked on two, cannot forget the contribution of those who lost eyes, arms, legs and even their minds in past conflicts. I cannot see how any group would back a move to lessen in any way the importance of our Remembrance day.
It is beyond my comprehension why some school officials, who have backed a move to abolish Remembrance Day as a school holiday, are still content to let the children out of school on days that have no significance to them, such as Victoria day which is not even recognized in England, the home of that gracious queen. It has been said that school children cannot understand the significance of Remembrance Day. Those who have fathers who were wounded or who died in past conflicts surely have some comprehension of it. If the others do not, it is time they were taught in the schools. A child's mind can comprehend much more difficult things than that.
I plead, therefore, with the government to lead this country in a more significant remembrance of those days in 1918 and 1945, so that Canadians do not fall into a lethargy in which praise of our dead becomes merely a sentimental practice.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I want to associate myself with previous speakers in tendering my most sincere congratulations to the hon. members for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) and Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Fortin) who respectively moved and seconded the address in reply.
As I am one of the first if not indeed the first, member from the provincec of Quebec to rise in this debate, I would reserve the

right to comment on certain parts of the speech made by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet.
In my humble opinion, the speech from the throne contains nothing which might restore that confidence and feeling of security given to the Canadian people by the former government.
Yet, in this period of uncertainty, the people of Canada had reasons to count on government action to solve, if not entirely, at least in part the problems we are facing.
I have listened with great attention to the speech which the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made last night and he left us with the impression that everything was going fine in this country. I wonder whether, if he had made the same speech before an audience made up of unemployed people or of farmers hard pressed to dispose of their products, he would have scored as much success as he did achieve in this house, before his numerous supporters.
I believe the picture drawn by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) gives a much better idea of the economic situation confronting us at this time. Unemployment is an evil which is still rampant in Canada, and our workers are in a situation they are helpless to relieve, since it is largely a responsibility of our leaders and it remains with the federal government to do something about it. In fact the federal government has recognized its share of responsibility, and brought down at least one measure designed to check that plague. I refer here to the action proposed by the right hon. Prime Minister shortly before his trip, and contained in a telegram which he sent to the premier of the province of Quebec, as well as to all the other premiers of the provinces of Canada, I suppose.
It was an offer by this government to take care of 50 per cent of the salaries and wages to be paid directly by municipalities to their contractors from December to April inclusive, on works which normally would not be undertaken in the wintertime.
On November 20 last, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) sent us copies of federal government proposals in connection with its program for promoting winter employment in our municipalities. The suggestions were contained in the copy of a letter addressed to the provincial premiers.
After considering that offer of encouragement by the federal government, our municipalities were alarmed at the scanty benefits
The Address-Mr. Racine provided by that federal assistance offered as an encouragement, and instead they gave way to despair.
The financial situation of our municipalities is most precarious, and we have only to glance at the statistics to realize that, far from getting better, the situation is getting worse. Thus, municipal liabilities which amounted to 466 million dollars in 1945, exceeded one billion dollars in 1956.

I must say, Mr. Speaker, that there is a huge difference between what government supporters said in 1957 and 1958 and what the government has done in many fields since it took power. What I just said applies most especially in the province of Quebec where, unfortunately, the keynote of both the 1957 and 1958 campaigns was a far cry from what it was in other provinces.
It is particularly true in the field of dominion-provincial relations. Throughout the electoral campaign of 1957, the Prime Minister and his colleagues at the time kept repeating that once in power they would immediately settle that question of the fiscal relations between the dominion and the provinces.
Before that period, on January 18, 1957, the present Prime Minister who was then leader of the opposition, dealt with the matter during a debate on a resolution to present legislation providing for the establishment of a council for the advancement of the arts, humanities and social sciences in Canada.
The Address-Mr. Roberge This is what he said, as can be seen in Hansard, page 400 of the English edition:
What is envisaged here will simply postpone the day. The whole question of dominion-provincial relations will have to be faced.
Criticizing the government of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, the then leader of the opposition added:
We simply postpone again facing the problem that must be faced in this country, a problem which cannot be faced by bits and pieces, but which must be faced at an early date.
Hence the promises and statements throughout the country on the matter, which I have mentioned before and which, as a matter of fact, my leader has discussed in his eloquent indictment of the government, last Monday.
What did the government do by way of keeping its promises? A conference was held on November 25 and 26, 1957, a little more than five months after the 1957 election, a conference which-so the Canadian people had been told-was to settle all taxation problems facing the federal government and the provinces. At that conference, the provinces made their representations and claims. At the end of the meeting, the Minister of Finance said it was impossible to grant what the provinces were asking. And, at that time, a solemn promise was made to the effect that a new conference would be held in January 1958.
What happened on that date? Has any conference been held in accordance with the promises made and the solemn pledge taken? On the contrary, a mere telegram, as was recalled by the Leader of the Opposition, was sent to the provincial premiers, saying: "Here is what the federal government is doing or has decided to do." A unilateral conference and, if I may add, a one-party conference. Were the provinces satisfied with that arrangement? Certainly not, if we go by the comments of the provincial leaders of that time. The same promises were made on the occasion of a new election. Did a new conference take place? Not at all.
The speech from the throne however tells us that the government intends to do something to solve those problems. But how are they doing it? Once again unilaterally. Let me quote the relevant part of the speech from the throne, on page 3 of Hansard. It reads:
My government will recommend an amendment to the Federal-Provincial Tax Sharing Arrangements Act to extend for another year the increase made last year in the provincial share of personal income tax revenue.

My government proposes that the entire subject of financial relations between the dominion and the provinces shall receive continued active co-operative study. All provincial governments are being asked to agree to the use, for this purpose, of the machinery of the existing federal-provincial continuing committee on fiscal and economic matters working under the direction of a committee consisting of the Minister of Finance and all provincial treasurers.
On the same day, January 15, the Prime Minister wrote to the premiers of the different provinces, simply quoting this sentence from the speech from the throne, and inviting the provincial treasurers to co-operate with the Minister of Finance within the continuing federal-provincial committee on fiscal and economic matters.
We are very far, Mr. Speaker, from the statement made by the then leader of the opposition on January 18, 1957, which I quoted earlier. Again, it is the statu quo; the government hesitates, takes indifferent action, and fails to face the problem squarely. These are new contradictions between election speeches and the action taken.
To this problem of fiscal relations, Mr. Speaker, is related another problem that is essential to our cultural development, that of the assistance to be given to the institutions of higher learning. I spoke briefly on that matter last year and I would like now to discuss it further, and express the opinion not of a jurist, but of a lawyer who thinks that constitutions are made to be changed rather than to remain static. I feel I should repeat now what I said last year. I refer to Hansard of May 22, 1958:
The right to education belongs first of all to our children and should not depend on the financial means of their parents but on the young people's talent and future opportunities. With regard to this right there is, of course a corresponding obligation on behalf of parents to provide this education. The state however should play a supplementary part, which belongs in the first place to the provinces.
However, in 1958, when science is fast developing, when artificial moons circle around the earth, when long range missiles can be launched farther and farther, education is becoming more and more an intercontinental problem, and at least an interprovincial problem. I do not see any reason why the central power should not contribute its share in this field, without infringing upon the rights of parents and of the provinces.
If we must give assistance to the children who want to go to university, it is also imperative to assist our universities themselves, which at the present time all complain of lack of funds.
In this respect, the Liberal government of the right honourable Louis St. Laurent had provided a sizeable financial help to universities; but, unfortunately, the universities of my province have been able to benefit from those grants only once.
And later, I said:
As far as the children are concerned, the federal government could, while respecting the autonomy


of the provinces as well as the rights of the parents in the field of education, as I have already said, give substantial assistance to those who have talent, as well as the will to succeed and to prepare adequately for the future. This government help could well be implemented through the agency of the national conference of Canadian universities. The government would then have no control whatever over anything save over the amounts which it could put at the disposal of that conference.
In this regard, Mr. Speaker, there is always that complicated problem of provincial autonomy in the field of education. It seems now that there is unanimity on that matter and that federal aid to the institutions of higher learning is not an infringement of provincial rights in matters of education since the provinces retain the right to control and supervise the establishment of institutions and the drawing up of programs in certain matters. Going back to September 4, 1958, we see that members of all parties voted the appropriations asked by the Minister of Finance for help to the universities. In fact, a vote was taken in committee and there was no dissenting voice.
Two days later, the Minister of Finance asked that this appropriation be increased by 50 cents per capita or from $1 as it stood, to $1.50. The hon. minister stated on that occasion that his government would always respect the autonomy of the provinces in this matter. This statement is in no way contrary to all the statements made in the past by the Right. Hon. Louis St. Laurent when this appropriation was introduced for the first time in 1951, and was voted every year thereafter.
Since 1951, therefore, all universities throughout the country have been able to receive from the central government, either directly or through the national conference of Canadian universities, or through the provinces, quite a substantial amount out of taxes collected by the central government. Therefore, we find that only the universities of the province of Quebec have been unable to receive their share, except in one instance.
From a practical point of view, the problem is therefore still with us, and I feel I must lay stress on two aspects of this problem, first the legal side, and second the practical side.
I read with close attention the brilliant speech made last year, on September 4, 1958, by my colleague from Hull (Mr. Caron)-

This speech contained a number of statements and quotations, and I do not intend to repeat these statements and these arguments here, although it might do some good to a certain member.
I wish, however, to put on the record a personal interpretation which I think is valid, whatever the hon. member for Roberval may think, and which, I trust, will be agreed to by all members of this house, and by all those who are interested in the matter of federal grants to institutions of higher learning.
It cannot be denied that the provinces have a fundamental right in the field of education. However, I believe it can truly be said and reiterated that all governments have the responsibility to give assistance.
On January 18, 1957, during that same debate I mentioned a moment ago, the Right Honourable Louis St. Laurent, in expressing his opinion on this matter, made the following statement as reported on page 398 of Hansard.
But at the same time we recognize that the wealth of the mind expressed in the arts, humanities and social sciences is not a private prerogative but may rightfully belong to all people who wish to seek for it. Therefore it seems to me that governments have a duty to assume some responsibility of providing not control and direction of the arts but leadership in making available the assistance which is so greatly needed.
When we look closely at Section 93 of the British North America Act, we have reason to believe that the fathers of confederation, in 1867, could not foresee and in fact did not foresee what the situation would be in 1950. Actually, the main paragraph provides that the legislatures shall be allowed to enact exclusively legislation in the field of education, on and in accordance with the following conditions. Four paragraphs follow, of which the first three refer to separate or dissident schools, and to school trustees. One readily realizes that, at the time, schools and not institutions of higher learning were considered. Besides, if I am not mistaken, universities at the time were private institutions. At least, it is a well known fact, in so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, where, for instance, Laval University had been established in 1852 by the Quebec Seminary. In 1867, that university had but a few faculties, namely Law, Medicine and Theology. Therefore, I repeat that in my opinion the fathers of confederation, in good faith, did not think in terms of universities, when section 93 was enacted.
The Address-Mr. Roberge
The following legal point is now raised: Has the federal government the right to levy taxes, and then earmark part of those funds to help universities? Or else, to put it differently, have the provinces alone the right to financially help institutions of higher learning?
I must say, at this point, that I am not approaching the matter from the standpoint of autonomy or centralization, but that I am merely trying to find new arguments to solve the problem. Section 91, paragraph 3, of the British North America Act, gives the following right to the central government:
The raising of money by any mode or system of taxation.
On the other hand, section 92, paragraph 2, gives the following right to the provinces:
Direct taxations within the province in order to the raising of revenue for provincial purposes.
Therefore, it seems that the provincial right of taxation is limited to the levying of funds for provincial purposes.
On the other hand, section 91, paragraph 3, makes no restriction.
Therefore, I believe that one may draw the conclusion that the federal government has always the right to financially help the provinces through subsidies-besides, that was one of the foundations of the con-federative act-and also to financially help the institutions located in the provinces.
This right may as a matter of fact be reversed, and nothing is said about a province not being entitled to help the institutions of the neighbouring provinces. In any way, this has been done in several cases. I do not think I am mistaken when I say that all funds provided by federal taxation are converted in the consolidated revenue fund. It is then up to this house to decide in which manner these funds will be distributed.
In concluding this part of my remarks, I hope that my fellow lawyers, particularly those from my province, will take my comments in good part, because I am making them in good faith. I also hope that my speech will not exclude any other discussion and I trust that others will also deal with the matter.
I am now coming to the practical side of the assistance for our universities. Is that assistance necessary or superfluous? May I quote again the resolution voted by the national conference of Canadian universities in 1956:
Resolved:	that the representatives of Canada,
having given full consideration to the matter, express the opinion that it is their responsibility to give urgent warning to the people of our country

The Address-Mr. Roberge that the problem facing the universities has taken the proportion of a serious national crisis, which is indeed jeopardizing the advance of our country and its place amongst the nations of the world. They also are of the opinion that only an immediate and vigorous intervention and the co-operation of all governments in our country, of business, industry and private employers will solve this problem.
I also would like to quote part of what Mr. N. M. A. MacKenzie said in "Government Support of the Universities":
From these important viewpoints, the universities are an essential element of our provincial institutions and therefore have to seek an important part of their financial resources on the local and provincial levels. However, it cannot be said that the work of a university is circumscribed by the boundaries of a province, neither with regard to its scope nor with regard to its significance. There is not a single great university in our country which does not take students from all provinces. In some eases, students coming from other provinces can make up a third of the student body. Likewise, the graduates of our universities are scattered throughout our national territory.
I shall not quote further for time is short. Consequently, it is undeniable that the universities lack not only money, space, and the necessary equipment for education but they also lack personnel.
In view of the arguments submitted and the extraordinary scientific development which has taken place, the federal government cannot turn a deaf ear to this appeal by the institutions of higher learning. The government and especially the Conservative members of the province of Quebec must do everything in their power so that the institutions of the province of Quebec may benefit from those funds which are at present available to them.
As the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent once said: "Quebec is a province like the other provinces." We recall how sharply he was criticized at the time by his opponents, especially in his own province.
"Quebec is a province like the other provinces", the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet stated last Friday. I am convinced that he does not regret that statement. I am also convinced that with his talent and his capacity for persuasion, he will succeed in persuading his colleagues really to set down to work and to solve that question which is so close to our hearts.
I remember that in the early part of last September, the member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) stated that federal assistance to institutions of higher learning could perhaps take the form of assistance to scientific research or to construction. The point is not to seek reasons for or means of evading the


question, but to consider it squarely with courage and with the same good faith which inspired the fathers of confederation in 1867.
We all hope to see a true form of Cana-dianism develop in this country. No particular group favours the assimilation of other groups, but all favour the enrichment of the nation through the diversity of cultural contributions.
If all are agreed that from a practical point of view, as was proved in this house last year, the federal government must do its share to help this enrichment process and to develop Canadian culture, there should, I think, be a way to reach unanimous agreement from a legal point of view.
I said that the Minister of Finance and the provincial treasurers have been asked to get together. When this happens, and I hope it will be soon, they will have to discuss this matter. If there is any doubt as to the interpretation to be given to the Canadian constitution, let us take the necessary means either to clarify it or to amend it accordingly.
Those who founded Canada in 1867 did not fear to take their responsibilities. We, their sons, and those who now direct the course of the nation and of the provinces, must not lack courage and refuse to find solutions.
When the matter is finally settled, Canadians, whatever their origin, will continue to live together, to enrich one another intellectually and will contribute to give this country the choice position it deserves.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on their clear thinking and on their clear delivery. I would like also to add my congratulations to the new members from Grenville-Dundas, Mont-magny-L'Islet and Springfield. Of course, I must include my friend and former opponent in Davenport, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). I regret that he is sitting on the Liberal side of the house but I hope that we may pursue our political differences on the floor of this house at the same high level that we were able to pursue them in the constituency of Davenport.
I note with some satisfaction, Mr. Speaker, the theme of the speech from the throne and that many of the hon. members who have spoken recognize the urgency and the importance of the threat of communism to our

way of life and also the importance of meeting the competition of Russia and her satellites. We must unfortunately accept the premise that the Russians intend to spread their version of communism throughout the world. It is not necessarily a struggle which will culminate in an armed conflict although we must be prepared for that military eventuality. The main issue will be on the economic and scientific front. When we consider the scientific and economic front, it is not my purpose at this time to count our many blessings but to speak briefly on two problems which show our system to disadvantage. The question is whether we can today by self-discipline, co-operative planning and hard work do what the Russians and communist China are doing by compulsion. In many ways we still maintain advantages. We start off with better economic conditions; the individual is given more respect.
The two problems which I wish specifically to mention are those of recurring unemployment and the needs of our educational system. It is not sufficient for the opposition to taunt us with not solving the unemployment problem in one year and a half. It is no answer for the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) to pussyfoot on both sides of the economic fence as to whether we should solve unemployment or inflation. The record of the former Liberal government is not such that they can sit back in a hypocritical and complacent attitude and heap ridicule on the present government. We recall the past crisis. The great depression is mentioned in the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, the depression of 1929 to 1933, the recession in 1937 and 1938, the recession in 1953 and 1954 and the recession that started in 1957. Who was in power at that time? The Liberals. Therefore, they knew unemployment was a recurring problem. Yet, in the 25 years, with their
The Address-Mr. Morton lengthy experience and their brain trust, they did nothing to solve either unemployment or inflation. Now they expect us to solve in one-half year what they could not do in 25 years. I thank them for the compliment of expecting us to be able to do it.
We cannot solve this problem, Mr. Speaker, by hurling abuse across the floor as to who is to blame.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am reminding hon. gentlemen opposite that when they hurl abuse at us they must look at their own record.
Our Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), with the co-operation of the various groups across the dominion, has been endeavouring to set up temporary work programs to ease the periodic unemployment. Our ministers have been on trade missions; they have been busy in trade conferences. However, Mr. Speaker, I think all of us must admit that public works programs, essential as they are, are not the entire answer. They are like an aspirin to deaden the pain of a headache but they do not solve the problem. I think there is a challenge, as there never was a challenge before, to the various labour leaders, industrial leaders, manufacturers and political leaders of all levels of government to sit down with specialists to consider the problems that create unemployment.
The problem is how to produce without pricing ourselves not only out of our own market but out of the markets of the world. Employment depends on trade and the ability to sell our services and products at competitive prices in Canada and abroad.
On motion of Mr. Morton the debate was adjourned.
